blocks.h: THE ONE YOU LOVE IS RIGHT HERE
Roya Publication No. 123
by Chew Z
THE BOOK BEFORE
Each of these books stands on its own, and you can start anywhere. The one before this was about a man and a voice in the dark.

Kian Rahimi was forty, and he had driven the 405 for eleven years, an hour each way, and never once minded, because he spent the hour inside other people’s books. He kept a list on his phone of every story that pulled its punch at the end, and he carried the darker version of each one in his head, the way it should have gone. He had never written a word of his own. He had a wife who listened better than anyone he knew, and a son of eight who built a radio station out of a dishwasher box in the hall and wanted, more than anything, to make something with his father. Kian kept saying later.

Then a friend put a jar in his hand at a party and laughed, and one night in the garage, with the lamp switched off, a voice began to tell him his own stories back, better than he had ever told them. He wrote them down. People who heard them pulled over on the freeway and cried.
It was a book about the muse, and what she gives, and what she takes in return. And it was about the one question a man in love with his own work never thinks to ask: where is all of it coming from?
SYNOPSIS

Every morning at nine, on Westwood Boulevard, an old man raises the steel shutter of his rug shop by hand, and as it rattles up into its drum he sings one line of an eight-hundred-year-old poem. O you who went away on pilgrimage, where are you, where are you? Everybody who knows that line knows the one that comes after it. He never sings it. It says: the one you love is right here.

Everybody lies. Mostly not the big lies. The small ones that hold a face in place, a dozen times a day: I’m fine. It’s going up. Nothing, just menus. And underneath all of them, older and quieter than the rest, the first lie of all, the one a person tells himself so early and so often that it stops sounding like a voice at all and starts sounding like silence.

Farzad Karimi breaks airplane parts for a living. He loads them, slowly, until they fail, and writes down exactly where they were weakest. He is a careful man, living in a borrowed house in Mar Vista under the paper-bark trees, three streets from the hill where on a clear evening you can see the sea, and the dead man who owned that house asked him to look after its money. There is an envelope at the bottom of the kitchen drawer now, under the takeout menus. Nobody else has read it.

Then the shortest night of the year, a neighbour’s wild garden under a net of little lights, and a kind stranger holding out a tin. For a few hours the fear switches off, a fear he never knew he was carrying, and in the silence it leaves behind he hears his own voice telling the truth for the first time in his life.
It is the first true thing he has said in two years. It will not be the last. It will not be the worst.
A NOTE FROM THE AUTHOR
I have come to believe that most of what we carry is not grief, or debt, or failure. It is the effort of not saying something.

A lie is rarely an act. It is a habit, and it nearly always begins at home, inside one person, long before it reaches anyone else. Where a person cannot quite love himself, there is a gap, an empty room, and lies are very good at filling empty rooms. They move in quietly. They take the energy that should have gone into living and spend it on upkeep: on keeping the story straight, the face in place, the drawer shut. First we lie to ourselves, because it is easier than looking. Then we lie to the people we love, because we have already decided what is true. By the time anyone else is hurt, the damage was done years before, in private, by a man who could not stand to hear his own voice.

This book is about one afternoon when that stops. A medicine, used carefully, in a quiet room, turns down the fear for a few hours, and a person hears what he has been saying underneath it. It does not make anyone tell the truth. It only takes away the reason not to. What surprised me, writing it, is how little else most of us would need.

So I keep asking a question the book cannot answer. What if every person got to feel that once, just once, in their life? One day without the hum of fear in the next room. One day to say the plain true thing to themselves, and then to the people at their table.

And why would something with that power be locked away from us? I know the honest answers. It can overheat a body and strain a heart. What is sold as it is often something else. It is not for everyone, and some people come out of it worse. The day after can be dark. Those are reasons for care, for doctors, for quiet rooms and kind company and the truth about the risks. I am still not sure they are reasons for a locked door. I would rather we argued about it in daylight than pretended the door was never there.

The family in this book, their neighbours and the woman in Ojai are invented. Mar Vista, its houses and its Sunday market, the drum circle at Venice, the valley at Ojai and its pink evening light are real, and so is the history of the medicine. The poem is Rumi’s, and its last line is the reason for the book: alas, that you yourselves are the veil over your own treasure.
Chew Z
I. UNNAMED

Mar Vista means sea view. Whoever named it was an optimist, or a salesman, or both, because from most of its streets you cannot see the sea at all. You see stucco and jade plants and the backs of other people’s garages. You see power lines strung from pole to pole like the lines of a music score with no music on them yet.

But if you walk up Grand View Boulevard on a clear evening, to where the road tips over the crest of the hill, you turn around and there it is. The whole west side of Los Angeles runs downhill in front of you, roofs and palms and the long straight cut of Venice Boulevard, and at the bottom of it all, past the last of the houses, a strip of light lies across the world like a blade laid on a table. That is the Pacific. On those evenings the name tells the truth.
We lived three streets from that hill for eleven years. I want to start there, on a Sunday in April, because that is the last day I can remember when nothing was wrong.

The market set up every Sunday morning on Grand View, just below Venice Boulevard, where the city closed the street and let the farmers in. By nine o’clock the road was a long tunnel of white canopies, and under them the whole of the neighbourhood came out in the clothes it wore to do nothing: men in sandals with coffee, women with dogs, babies in slings, a boy with a guitar playing the same three songs he played every week and playing them a little better every week. There were strawberries from Oxnard that smelled red before you could see them. There was a man who sold honey in jars marked with the names of the hills it came from, and a woman who sold eggs in colours I did not know eggs came in, blue and olive and a brown so deep it was almost purple.
My daughter Yasi was eleven that spring. She walked ahead of us with her grandfather’s hand in one of hers and a paper cone of kettle corn in the other, explaining the eggs to him.
“The blue ones are from a chicken called an Araucana [ar-ow-KAH-nuh],” she said, carefully, the way she had practised it. “From Chile. It’s genetic.”

“Genetic,” said Mansour, very seriously. He was seventy-two and wore a tweed cap in all weathers, and he bent his head to her when she talked as if she were telling him the price of gold. “And they taste blue?”

“Baba. No. They taste like eggs.” She called him Baba [BAH-bah], which is what Mina called him too, and what every Persian child calls a father; to a grandchild it is simply the shorter, warmer half of Bābā-bozorg [BAH-bah bo-ZORG], big father.
“Then what is the point of them?”
“The point,” Yasi said, with enormous patience, “is that they’re beautiful.”

He stopped walking. He looked at the eggs in their cardboard nest, the blue ones and the olive ones and the almost-purple ones, for a long moment, the way he looked at a rug someone had brought into his shop to sell, turning it a little toward the light.

“Yes,” he said. “That is a good point. That is the best point there is.” And he bought a dozen of the blue ones, which none of us ate, and which sat in a bowl on our kitchen counter for a week like a nest of small skies.

Mina walked beside me with her arm through mine. She had her father’s eyes, dark and heavy-lidded and amused, and her mother’s hands, which I had never seen except in photographs. She was wearing the green scarf she wore to the market every week, because, she said, a market is a party and you dress for a party.
“Look at them,” she said quietly.

I looked. The old man and the girl, a head of white hair and a head of black, bent together over a table of honey, arguing in Persian about which hill tasted best. Yasi’s Persian was a child’s Persian, full of English where the words ran out, and Mansour answered every English word with the Persian one, gently, without correcting her, just laying it down beside hers like a second coin.
“He’s happy,” I said.
“He’s happy here.” Mina leaned her head against my shoulder for a moment as we walked. “Do you know how long it took him? To be happy anywhere?”

I did know. Or I knew the story, the way you know the stories of the people you marry: the outline, told at dinners, worn smooth by telling. Mansour Sadri had come to Los Angeles in the spring of 1979 with one suitcase, after the revolution, a man of twenty-nine who had been rich in Tehran on Tuesday and had nothing by the end of the week. He had built a rug shop on Westwood Boulevard from a single folded carpet on a borrowed table. He had raised Mina alone after her mother died. He had bought a house in Mar Vista when Mar Vista was a place nobody wanted, and he had lived long enough to see it become a place everybody did.
That was the story as it was told. There were parts of it that were not told, and I did not know yet that there were.

At the end of the market, where Grand View met the next street down, there was always the same stall: a long table under no canopy at all, covered with bowls and cups the colour of river stones. The woman behind it was in her sixties, brown as a saddle, with grey hair in a braid down to her waist and no shoes. Her name was Sunny. She lived two doors down from us, in a house with a kiln in the garage and wind chimes on every eave, and she had been in Venice, she said, since Venice was a place where you could get your head broken for having long hair, and in Mar Vista since Venice got too expensive for people like her.
“Mansour,” she said. “My handsome man.”

“Sunny jān,” he said. Jān [JAHN] is what you say in Persian to someone you hold dear; it means life, as in my life, and he put it after her name the way he put it after everybody’s, the mailman’s, the dentist’s. “You are selling the same bowls as last week.”
“They’re new bowls. They look the same because I’m consistent.”

He picked one up and turned it in his hands. It was a plain thing, rough on the outside and glazed inside a deep sea-green, with a single thumbprint pressed into the rim where she had held it while it was wet.
“This one,” he said. “The one with the mistake.”
“That’s not a mistake. That’s my thumb.”
“I know,” said Mansour. “That’s why I want it.”
The house was the second thing Mansour ever loved in America, after Mina, and in some ways, I think, he trusted it more.

It stood in a part of Mar Vista that people who know about such things call the Tract. In 1948, when the soldiers had come home from the war and needed somewhere to live, an architect named Gregory Ain built fifty-two small houses on three quiet streets here, all at once, for ordinary families. They were not the houses ordinary families were used to. They were low and plain and modern, flat-roofed, with whole walls of glass that faced the gardens instead of the street, and inside, the walls between some of the rooms could fold or slide away, so that a family could open its whole house into one room in the daytime and close it into small private rooms at night. A landscape designer named Garrett Eckbo had planted every street with a single kind of tree, so that each street had its own shade and its own smell in the evening. Ours, Moore Street, was lined with melaleucas [mel-uh-LOO-kuz], tall pale paper-bark trees from Australia that dropped their bark in long curling strips, like paper, and in summer the whole block smelled faintly of medicine and honey.

People had laughed at those houses in 1948. Some of the buyers had added pitched roofs and plaster shutters, to make them look like real houses. By the time Mansour bought ours, in 1986, half the street had been ruined that way, and ours had not, and he took that as a sign.

“Look,” he told me, the first time Mina brought me home to meet him. It was 2001, and I was twenty-two, and terrified of him. He walked me through the house as if it were a museum and he the only guard. “You see the wall? The glass? The garden comes inside. In Tehran, in the old houses, the garden is the middle of the house, and the rooms are around it, and the house looks in, at the garden, not out, at the street. This man understood that. An American. In 1948.” He folded back the wooden partition between the living room and the room beside it, and closed it, and opened it again, like a boy with a new toy. “A house that can change its shape. A house that does not lie about what it is.”
I had no idea what he meant. I nodded as though I did.

He was not an easy man to stand next to in those days. He was courteous to me in the way that a wall is courteous: it lets you lean on it, it does not fall on you, and you are never in any doubt about which of you is the wall. He asked me what my father did. He asked me what I earned. He asked me — in Persian, to Mina, in front of me, as if I could not understand, though he knew perfectly well I could — whether I was the kind of man who would ever need to be looked after.
“Baba,” Mina said, very quietly. Just the one word.

He looked at her. Something passed between them that I was not part of. Then he turned to me and smiled, and the smile was real, and I liked him enormously for the rest of his life, and I was afraid of him for most of it.

That night, on the drive back to my apartment, Mina said, “He said something to me when I was very small. I don’t remember the day, I just remember the sentence. He said it more than once.” She was looking out of the window at Venice Boulevard going by, the closed shops, the long dark median where, she said, the old red streetcars used to run all the way down to the sea. “He said, You will never need anyone. I will make sure of it.”
“That’s a nice thing for a father to say.”
“Is it?” she said. And then she laughed, and said it was, of course it was, and put her cold hand on the back of my neck while I drove.

We married in that garden a year later, under the paper-bark trees, with Mansour’s rugs laid on the grass so the guests’ feet would not get wet. When Yasi was born, nine years after that, and our apartment in Culver City had become a box with a crying baby in it, Mansour came over one Sunday, looked around the box for a long time without speaking, and said, “Come home.”

So we came home. It was his house. It had his name on the deed and his photograph on the wall in the hall: a young man in a narrow black suit, standing alone outside a shop with a single rug hanging in the window behind him, squinting into a Los Angeles sun as if he did not yet trust it. Mansour lived in the little back bedroom off the garden that Gregory Ain had drawn for a child, and he would not hear of taking the big room. He paid the property tax. We paid for the food and the electricity and everything else, and I told myself that this was fair, and most days I believed it.

Every morning of his working life he drove to Westwood, to the shop on Westwood Boulevard between a Persian bookstore and a bakery that sold rosewater pastries in the shape of tiny shoes. And every morning, at nine o’clock exactly, he raised the steel shutter over the window by hand, the rattling, clanking old kind of shutter that rolled up into a drum, and as he raised it, he sang. Always the same line. Mina said he had sung it every morning since 1980.
Ey qowm be hajj rafteh, kojāyid, kojāyid… [AY GHOWM beh HAJ raf-TEH, ko-jah-YEED, ko-jah-YEED]

It is the first line of a poem by Rumi [ROO-mee], the Persian poet who lived eight hundred years ago and is still, somehow, the poet that half the people in Los Angeles have a line of on a mug. It means: O you people who went away on pilgrimage — where are you? Where are you? And the line that comes after it, which Mansour never sang aloud at the shutter but which everybody who knew the first line knew was coming, says: The one you love is right here. Come back. Come back.
I asked him once why that poem. Why every morning.
He was polishing his glasses on the end of his tie. He held them up to the light and looked through them at me.
“Because I went a long way to find something,” he said, “and it was in my own house the whole time.”
“What was?”
He put his glasses back on. “Ask me when you are older,” he said. I was thirty-eight.

There was one other thing he did every year that nobody explained to me. Each spring, on a weekday in April, he closed the shop for a day, which he never did otherwise, not for illness, not for Nowruz [no-ROOZ], the Persian New Year, and drove north alone, up the coast and inland, to a small town in the hills called Ojai [OH-hy]. He left before light and came home after dark, and if you asked him where he had been he said, To see an old friend, and if you asked him which friend he said, An old one, and smiled, and that was the end of it. Mina said he had done it every April of her life.
On Sunday evenings in summer we went to the sea.

You could walk it from our house, if you wanted to, though nobody did: forty minutes down Venice Boulevard and across Lincoln and through the last tangled streets before the beach. We rode bikes instead, Mina and Yasi and I, down the long flat green path along Ballona [buh-YOH-nuh] Creek, a concrete channel where a river used to run before the city poured it into a box, which herons stood in anyway, on one leg, as if they had not been told. The path follows the creek all the way out to where it meets the ocean, between the long rock breakwaters of the marina, and the smell changes as you go, from cut grass to tar to salt, so that you know with your eyes shut how close you are getting.
Then north along the bike path on the sand, past the volleyball nets and the old men fishing off the jetties, to Venice.

Venice on a Sunday evening is the loudest, kindest, most ridiculous place I know. The boardwalk is a mile of people selling things nobody needs, incense and sunglasses and paintings of the boardwalk, and people doing things nobody asked for: a man on roller skates playing the electric guitar, a man in a turban on roller skates playing nothing, a woman who would write your name on a grain of rice. There is a basketball court where the games are better than television, and an outdoor gym fenced in like a zoo enclosure where enormous oiled men lift enormous weights for an audience of tourists, and they know they are an audience and they love it. And at the end of the day, on the sand near the foot of Horizon Avenue, there is the drum circle.

Nobody runs it. Nobody started it, as far as anyone can tell you. Every Sunday afternoon since some time before anybody’s memory, people simply come to that patch of sand with drums, any drums, bongos and big African djembes and plastic buckets and one man with a car’s hubcap he hits with a spoon, and they sit in a rough ring and they play. Nobody leads. Somebody starts a rhythm and somebody else answers it, and in a while the whole ring has found the same beat without anyone deciding what it should be, and people who are not drumming begin to dance in the middle, badly and happily and without asking anyone’s permission. And they keep it up until the sun goes down into the sea.

Yasi loved it more than anything in the world. She had been dancing in that ring since before she could walk properly; we had photographs of her at two, in a sunhat and a nappy, holding the hands of a very tall man with dreadlocks to his knees. That summer, at eleven, she had decided she was too old to dance in front of her parents, and so she danced in front of us anyway, at the far side of the ring, where she could pretend we were not there.
Mina and I sat on the sand at the edge with our shoes off.
“Do you know what I like about this?” she said.
“The smell of the hubcap man?”

“Nobody’s in charge.” She drew a circle in the sand with her finger. “Nobody’s keeping count. Nobody’s ahead. You just come and you hit something and it’s fine.” She brushed the sand off her hands. “I grew up in a house where everything was counted. Every rug. Every dollar. My father knew to the dollar what everything we owned was worth, always, in his head. He used to say the number out loud at dinner sometimes, like a prayer. We are worth this much now. I used to think that was what a family was. A number you were all inside.”
She did not often talk about this. I put my arm around her.
“What do you think a family is now?”
She watched Yasi, who was spinning in the middle of the ring with her arms out and her eyes shut, her black hair flying out level with her shoulders.
“That,” she said.

The sun went down. It went down the way it does there in summer, slowly and then all at once, a red coin sliding into a slot. The drums went on for a while in the dark, slower now, and somebody lit a fire in a steel bin, which you are not allowed to do, and nobody stopped them. The light from the boardwalk came on behind us, and the smell of grilled corn and sage and salt, and the long hiss of the waves coming in and going out under all of it.

I was forty-three that summer. I tested airplane parts for a living, at a company in El Segundo, ten minutes south along the coast. My job was to take a thing that somebody else had designed — a bracket, a hinge, a piece of a wing — and put it in a machine and load it, slowly, more and more, until it broke. Then I wrote down exactly how much it had carried, and exactly where it gave way, and why. People think it is a strange job when I tell them. It is the most honest job I know. A part does not pretend. It holds, or it does not, and when it fails it tells you precisely where it was weakest, and it is never offended to be asked.
I sat on the sand that night with my wife’s head on my shoulder and my daughter dancing in the firelight, and I thought — I remember thinking it, in those words — this will hold.
That last winter he brought home a rug.

A small one, old, rolled under his arm like a newspaper. He unrolled it on the dining table for Mina one evening in February: a Kashan [kah-SHAHN], from the old weaving city of that name, a garden pattern, a vase in the middle with flowers coming out of it in every direction, the reds gone soft as wine. One corner was torn, the threads hanging loose.
“For a friend,” he said. “Can you make it so nobody knows?”
Mina turned the corner to the light and studied it with her father’s own look. “Nobody but me,” she said.

She mended it over three weekends, out in the garden, with her curved needle and a thread the colour of pomegranate seeds, and when it was done you could not see where the tear had been. Mansour ran his thumb over the corner, again and again, and did not say anything, and kissed the top of her head. In April, on his day, he took it with him to Ojai, and he came home without it.
He died in July, on a Thursday, at the shop.

He had raised the shutter that morning and sung his line, the man in the rosewater bakery next door told us later, and gone inside and made his tea in the little brass samovar [SAM-uh-var], the tall urn that keeps the water hot all day, at the back, and sat down in the big chair among the folded rugs to drink it, the way he had every morning for forty years. When his assistant came in at ten he was still sitting there, with the glass of tea on the arm of the chair, full and cold. The doctor said his heart had simply stopped, between one breath and the next, and that he would not have known.

Mina did not cry at the hospital. She did not cry at the mosque in Westwood, or at the cemetery on the hill above Culver City where we buried him the next morning, as soon as they would let us, which is the custom. She stood at the grave in a black scarf with her hands folded in front of her and her face perfectly still, and accepted the hands of three hundred people, old men from the rug trade, women from the bakery, a city councilman, the man with the honey from the market, and Sunny, barefoot even there, who held Mina’s face in both her hands and said nothing at all.

She cried four days later, at home, in the kitchen, because she opened the cupboard and saw the bowl. Sunny’s bowl, the sea-green one with the thumbprint in the rim. He had kept his sugar cubes in it.

I held her on the kitchen floor for most of an hour. Yasi came in once and stood in the doorway and then came and sat down on the floor too, on the other side of her mother, and the three of us sat there, on the cold tiles, in our socks, while the light moved across the floor and up the cupboard doors and went orange and then went.
“He was always so sure,” Mina said at last. Her voice was wrecked. “About everything. He was so sure he’d see to everything. And now —” She stopped.
“Now what?”
She shook her head against my chest.

The forty days passed — in our tradition you mourn hard for forty days, and on the fortieth the family gathers one more time, and after that you are supposed to begin, slowly, to live again — and on the forty-first day a lawyer came to the house. A small, tidy, kind man from Encino, who had been Mansour’s lawyer for thirty years and who sat at our dining table with his papers squared in front of him and a glass of tea he did not drink, exactly where Mansour used to sit.

The house was Mina’s now, he said. Paid off, entirely, since 1998. Its value at the present time — he named a figure, and I watched Mina’s face not move. The shop’s lease, the stock of rugs, which a dealer in Beverly Hills had already offered to buy. And there was an investment account. Mansour had been putting money into it, the lawyer said, a little every month, for thirty-five years. Never spending from it. Never touching it. He named that figure too.
Mina said nothing at all. She was looking out through the glass wall, at the garden, at the lemon tree her father had planted the year he bought the house, which had grown taller than the roof.
“There is also this,” the lawyer said, and he slid an envelope across the table. Not to her. To me.

My name was on it, in Mansour’s careful, slanting English hand, the hand of a man who had learned to write a second alphabet at twenty-nine and never quite trusted it. Inside there was one sheet of paper, folded in three.
Farzad jān, it said. She will tell you she does not need you to look after the money. She will be right. Look after it anyway. — M.S.
That was all.

I read it twice. I passed it to Mina, and she read it, and her mouth did something complicated, and she put the letter face down on the table and laid her hand on top of it, flat, the way you put your hand over a glass to keep something in or keep something out.
“Well,” she said. “You heard him.”

The lawyer left. Yasi was at a friend’s. We sat in the dining room, in the long gold evening, with the partition slid open so that the whole house was one room, and the garden coming in through the glass, and the paper-bark trees along the street stirring in the wind off the sea.
“I don’t know anything about investing,” I said.
“You’re an engineer.”
“I break airplane parts.”

“You know how much things can carry.” She turned her hand over, on top of the letter, and held mine. “That’s all money is, Farzad. It’s just how much a family can carry.” She smiled at me, the first real smile since the shop, tired and wet and full of something I took for trust. “I’ll set it all up. The passwords, the logins, so we can both see it. And then it’s yours. I don’t want to look at it. I mean it. I’ve been looking at that number my whole life. I’m done.”
“Mina —”
“Please,” she said. “Let it be yours.”
I said yes.

I want to be very clear about that, because of everything that came after. Nobody forced it on me. Nobody tricked me. A dead man asked me, and the woman I loved asked me, and I wanted to be asked. I wanted, more than I had wanted anything in a long time, to be the one in that house who carried something.
I said yes, and I meant it, and I believed, that evening, with the whole of my careful engineer’s heart, that I knew exactly how much I could carry before I broke.
For the first year I did everything right.

I read books. I read the kind of books that have a picture of an old man on the cover and the word wealth in the title, and they all said the same thing, which was that a man like me should do nothing. Buy the whole market, they said, a little piece of every big company in America, in one cheap fund, and leave it there, and do not look at it, and in twenty years you will be richer than if you had been clever. I liked that. It sounded like an engineer’s answer: the plain part that holds, not the clever part that cracks.

So I moved Mansour’s money, slowly, into the plain part, and I did not look at it. Or I looked at it on Sundays only, after the market, with coffee, the way some men read the sports pages. The number went up a little, and down a little, and up. It was fine. It was boring. Mina never once asked to see it, and when I offered to show her, on the first anniversary of her father’s death, she put her hand over the screen of my phone, gently, and said, “I believe you.”
The trouble started with a boy at work.

He was not really a boy. He was twenty-six, a young engineer who had the bench next to mine in the test hall, a long cold hangar of a room where the machines stood in rows like the skeletons of animals. He was clever and pleasant and he wore the same grey hooded sweatshirt every day, and at lunch he sat with his phone flat on the table in front of him and watched a line on the screen go up and down, and sometimes he laughed out loud at it, and sometimes he went very quiet.
“What is that?” I asked him one day.

“Calls,” he said. He turned the phone so I could see. “I bought the right to buy a chip company at a set price. If it goes past that price by Friday, I make a lot. If it doesn’t, I lose what I paid for the right.” He shrugged. “It’s not gambling. It’s leverage.”

Leverage is an engineer’s word. It is a lever: a long bar, a small push at one end, a heavy thing lifted at the other. I knew all about levers. I also knew, though I did not think of it then, that the longer the lever, the less it takes to snap it.
“How much did you pay?” I said.
“Four hundred bucks.”
“And if it goes past the price?”
He smiled. “Then it’s not four hundred bucks.”

On the Friday, it went past the price. He showed me the screen at four o’clock, and when the number came up there was a little burst of light on it, a spray of tiny coloured sparks that came out from the middle and faded, like the very end of a firework, like something being celebrated. He had turned four hundred dollars into six thousand in five days.
That night, when Mina and Yasi were asleep, I sat in the dark kitchen and downloaded the same app.

I want to describe it truthfully. Nothing happened to me that night. I did not feel greed, or fever. I felt curiosity, which is the oldest and most respectable thing an engineer feels. How does this work? What does it carry? I moved five thousand dollars out of the boring fund and into the app — five thousand out of more than a million, a rounding error, a loose screw — and I bought the right to buy a company that made computer chips, at a set price, by the end of the next month. And then I closed the phone and went to bed and lay awake until two, listening to the trees along the street rustle and drop their paper bark on our roof in the wind off the sea.

It went up. Of course it went up. That was the summer of 2023, when everything that had anything to do with computers went up, and kept going up, as if the whole country had decided at once that the future had arrived. In three weeks my five thousand dollars was nineteen thousand. When I sold it, the little burst of light went off on my screen, in the dark, in the bathroom at work, where I had gone to look at it alone.

I stood in a toilet stall in El Segundo with my phone in my hand, and I felt something open in my chest that I had not felt since I was a boy. Not money. I had never cared very much about money. It was the feeling of being right. Of having seen something before other people saw it. Of having pushed the small end of a long lever and watched the heavy world move.
I did not tell Mina. I told myself I was waiting until I had something finished to show her. I told myself it would be a surprise.

That August, for Yasi’s twelfth birthday, I bought her the bike she wanted, the good one, the one we had said was too expensive, and Mina raised her eyebrows at me across the cake and I winked at her. That was all. I winked. It was the first lie, and it did not feel like a lie. It felt like a present.
There is a kind of option that dies the same day you buy it. Traders call it, simply, a same-day option.

You buy it in the morning, and by four o’clock in the afternoon, New York time, which is one o’clock in Los Angeles, it is either worth something or it is worth nothing at all. There is no next week. There is no waiting it out. It is a bet on which way the whole American market will move before lunch. In those years it became the most popular thing in the world to trade, and you can understand why, if you have ever stood at a slot machine. It is fast. It is clean. You know by one o’clock. And the price is so small, and the possible win so large, that every single morning feels like a door standing a little bit open.
I started buying them in the winter. Small amounts. Then less small.

I want to tell you how it felt, because I have heard people talk about men like me as if we were stupid, and I was not stupid. I knew the numbers. I could have told you, to the decimal point, that most people who trade like this lose, and that the people who sell these things to us are not in the business of losing. I knew it the way you know smoking is bad for you. It was true, and it was over there, and it had nothing to do with the feeling in my hands at nine in the morning with the coffee going cold beside me.
Because the feeling was this: I was almost right. I was almost right all the time.

You lose, and you look at the line on the chart, and you see that if you had only waited ten minutes, or bought ten minutes earlier, or chosen the price one step higher, you would have won. You were close. The machine tells you every day how close you were. So it does not feel like losing. It feels like nearly winning. And nearly winning does something to a man’s chest that winning never does, because winning is over, and nearly is a promise.

I traded in the bathroom at work. I traded in the car in the parking structure before I went in, with the engine off. I traded on Sundays at the market, standing behind Yasi while she argued with the honey man about which hill tasted best, with my phone held low against my leg. When I lost, I bought more, to win it back, and when I won it back I bought more, because I was clearly on a run. I stopped moving money back into the boring fund. Then I started moving money out of it.
Mina noticed something. Not the money. Me.

“You’re somewhere else,” she said one night in bed. The window was open and the street was quiet, the kind of quiet the Tract has at night, with the paper-bark trees standing over the road and the far-off sound of the 405 like the sea.
“I’m tired. The new wing test.”

“Mm.” She lay on her back, looking at the ceiling. “Baba used to go somewhere else too. When I was little. He’d sit at dinner and his eyes would be counting.” She turned her head on the pillow and looked at me. “Is it the money? Is it too much? Having it?”
My heart stopped. Then started.
“No,” I said. “It’s fine. It’s boring. It’s going up.”

She looked at me a moment longer. Then she said, “Okay,” very softly, and turned on her side, away from me, and after a while I heard her breathing change, and I lay beside her in the dark and opened my phone under the sheet and looked at the number, which was not going up, which had not gone up in a long time.

There was a Monday in August of 2024 when the whole world sold at once. It started in Tokyo while Los Angeles was asleep, and by the time I woke up and looked at my phone it had come round the world like a wave, and every screen in every bathroom in America was red. I had bet a great deal, that Friday, that the market would go up on Monday morning. I had bet a quarter of everything that was left.

I sat in the car in the parking structure at El Segundo with the engine off and watched it go to nothing in eleven minutes. There was no burst of light. There is no light, when you lose. The number just gets smaller, and then it is a zero, and the zero is very small and grey and polite, and it sits there.

I went into work. I broke a wing bracket. It failed at precisely the load the designers had said it would, in precisely the place they had predicted, and I wrote it all down in my neat engineer’s hand and initialled the page, and I remember thinking, as I initialled it, at least something in the world is honest.
By the spring of 2025 Mansour’s money was gone.

Not all of it, not on paper. There were a few thousand dollars left in the boring fund, like the last coins at the bottom of a jar, enough to make the account look alive if you glanced at it. But the money he had put in a little every month for thirty-five years, the money that had been the number Mina grew up inside, was gone, and I had done it, in a bathroom, with my thumb.

There is a thing that happens then. I have read since that it happens to almost everyone. You do not stop. Stopping would mean the loss was real. Stopping would mean you had to say it. As long as you keep going, it is not a loss, it is a position, a hole you are in the middle of climbing out of, and all you need, all you need, is one good month.
All I needed was money to climb with.

The house was paid off. That was the thing about the house. It had been paid off since 1998, it was worth more than Mansour could ever have dreamed when he bought it, and it was sitting there, every night, holding us, asking for nothing. A bank will lend you money against a house like that. They call it a line of credit. You do not have to use it. It just sits there, like a spare tyre, in case of trouble.
I brought the papers home in April. The house was in both our names now; Mina had seen to that, the month after the lawyer, without my asking. So she had to sign.

We sat at the dining table where Mansour used to sit. It was evening, and the partition was open, and the garden was coming in through the glass, and the lemon tree was in flower, and the whole house smelled of it, that sweet heavy white smell that is almost too much, like a church at a wedding.

“It’s just for emergencies,” I said. “It doesn’t cost anything unless you use it. Everybody with a house like this has one. If the roof goes. If something happens to one of us.” I was talking too much. I could hear myself talking too much. “It’s just sensible.”

Mina read the first page. Then the second. She read slowly; she always read everything. Then she looked up at me across the table, and for a moment she looked so much like her father that I nearly said it, nearly said everything, right there, with the lemon flowers in the air.
“Okay,” she said.

She signed. Her signature was small and upright and neat, like her mother’s in the old photographs. She slid the papers back across the table to me and stood up and went to the kitchen to make tea, and did not say anything else, and I sat with the papers in front of me and my heart going like a hammer, and I thought that I had never loved anyone so much and I had never been so afraid.
That was the week the tariffs came.

I do not need to tell you about that week; you will remember it, if you were watching. Every day a new number from Washington, and every day the market went down, and then on one afternoon it went up further than it had in years, in an hour, because of a single sentence, and then it went down again. It was the best weather for a man like me that there had ever been. Everything was moving. Every morning the door stood wide open.

By Christmas, the line of credit was used to the last dollar. By January, I could not make the payments on it, because the payments were more than I earned. In February I missed the first one. In March I missed the second. The letters began to come, polite letters and then less polite ones, and I took the mail from the box every evening before anyone else could, and I read each letter standing in the driveway, and I folded it in three, the way Mansour’s letter to me had been folded, and I put it in my jacket.
I was not sleeping. I was going up the hill.

At night, after Mina was asleep, I would put on my shoes in the dark and walk up Grand View to the top, past the shut market street, past the dark houses with their cars parked nose to tail, to the crest where the road tips over and the city falls away to the sea. At night the sea is not a blade of light. It is the place where the lights stop. The whole west side glittering, block after block, orange and white and the red blink of planes going down into the airport, and then, at the bottom, a line, and past the line nothing, a black so complete it looks like a hole cut in the world.

I would stand there and look at the place where the lights stopped. I did not think anything. I just looked. And then I would walk home and lie down beside my wife and look at the ceiling until it went grey.
One hundred and sixty-six days.

That is how long there was, from the day the big envelope came to the morning they sold the house on the courthouse steps. I did not know the number on the day. I have counted it since, many times, the way you run your tongue over a broken tooth.

It came on a Thursday, the second of April. A large white envelope, heavier than the others, addressed to both of us, from a company I had never heard of in a city I had never been to. I opened it in the driveway, in the dusk, with the paper-bark trees moving over my head and somebody’s sprinkler ticking two gardens down.
NOTICE OF DEFAULT AND ELECTION TO SELL UNDER DEED OF TRUST.

I had to read it three times. It is written so as not to be understood. But under all the language it said a simple thing, and the simple thing was this: you owe us money you have not paid. You have ninety days to pay all of it. If you do not, we will set a date, and on that date we will sell your house to whoever is standing on the steps of the county courthouse with the most money, and you will leave.

There is a drawer in our kitchen, the one by the back door, where every family keeps the things that have nowhere else to go. Takeout menus. Rubber bands. Batteries that may or may not be dead. A birthday candle shaped like the number seven. I opened that drawer and put the envelope in, at the bottom, under the menus, and shut it. Then I went inside, and Yasi was doing her homework at the dining table with her headphones on, fourteen now and taller than her mother, singing very quietly to herself under her breath, and Mina was in the garden, kneeling on an old rug in the last of the light, mending the edge of somebody else’s carpet with a curved needle and a thread the colour of pomegranate seeds.
“Hi,” she said, without looking up.
“Hi.”
“Anything in the mail?”
“Just menus,” I said.

That night I did not go up the hill. I sat at the dining table after everyone had gone to bed, in Mansour’s place, with the house open around me, the long glass wall black and full of my own reflection, and I did the arithmetic. I am good at arithmetic. I did it in pencil on the back of a takeout menu, the way I would work out a load: what the account had been on the day the lawyer came, what was left, what the line of credit had been, what I owed, what I had lost, all of it, every column, every carry. I drew a line under it. I wrote the number.
Then I looked at it until the pencil marks stopped meaning anything.

I want to say that I said it then. That I sat at the table where her father had sat and said the number out loud to the empty house, the way he used to say his numbers at dinner like a prayer. I did not. I could not. Every time I opened my mouth to say it, my throat shut, as if there were a hand on it, and the hand was my own.
I tore the menu into very small pieces and put them in the bin under the sink, under the coffee grounds.
The next morning I went to work and broke something and wrote it down.
Sunny had a party every year on the shortest night.

“The longest day,” Mina corrected me, the first year we went. “It’s the summer solstice. The longest day, the shortest night. Sunny says you have to stay up for the whole of the dark or the year doesn’t turn properly.”
“Is that a Venice thing?”
“It’s a Sunny thing.”

That year the solstice fell on a Sunday, so the party was the Saturday night, the twentieth of June. Yasi was sleeping over at a friend’s in Palms. Mina had one of her headaches, the kind that start behind the left eye in the afternoon and lay her flat in a dark room by evening, and she lay in our bed with a wet cloth over her face and said, “Go. Please. Somebody from this house should go, she’ll be hurt.”
So I went alone, two doors down, at nine o’clock, with a bottle of wine I had bought on the card I was not supposed to be using.

Sunny’s back garden was the opposite of ours. Where ours was Mansour’s — clipped, ordered, a lawn, a lemon tree, a single bench — hers was a jungle that had been allowed to win. Bamboo and banana plants and a fig tree as wide as a room, and morning glory climbing over everything, and in the middle a cracked old patio of terracotta tiles with a fire pit, and strings of little warm lights criss-crossing overhead from the house to the garage to the fig tree, like a net thrown over the whole garden to hold it down. The garage door was rolled up, and the kiln stood in there, a squat brick box like a small church, still ticking as it cooled. There were bowls everywhere. Bowls on the tables with chips and olives in them, bowls on the walls as lamps, bowls hung in the fig tree with candles inside.

There were maybe forty people. Most of them were Sunny’s age, people who had been young in Venice when Venice was cheap: men with grey ponytails and women with silver rings on every finger, a retired surfer with a face like a walnut, a couple who had run a bookshop on the boardwalk for thirty years. And some younger ones, their children, or nobody’s children, people from the canyon and the beach who knew Sunny from the market. Somebody was playing a guitar by the fire pit, not well. Somebody else had a drum. It smelled of woodsmoke and sage and jasmine and something sweeter under it, like burnt sugar.

“Farzad!” Sunny came across the patio with her arms wide, barefoot, in a long dress the colour of rust, with a crown of something leafy on her grey head. She took my face in both her hands, the way she had taken Mina’s at the funeral. “Where’s my girl?”
“Headache. She sends her love.”
“And the angel?”
“Sleepover.”

“So it’s just you.” She held my face a moment longer and looked at me, really looked, with her small bright eyes, and something in her face changed. “Oh, honey,” she said quietly. “What’s happened to you?”
“Nothing. Work.”
“Mm.” She let go of my face and patted my cheek, twice, lightly. “Well. It’s the shortest night. You don’t have to carry anything tonight. Put it down. Have a drink. Look at the lights.”

I had a drink. I had two. I stood at the edge of the fire with a glass of my own bad wine and nodded at the surfer while he told me about a wave he had caught in 1979, and I thought about the drawer by the back door, and about the ninety days, of which nearly eighty were gone. That afternoon, while Mina slept, I had taken the big envelope out from under the menus, and I had not put it back. It was in my jacket now, against my chest, like a hand.

Around eleven, a man I did not know came round the circle by the fire with a small tin. He was perhaps sixty, bald, with a soft kind face and reading glasses pushed up on his head, and he was holding the tin open the way you hold out a dish of nuts. Inside it there were a few capsules, plain, the colour of sand.
“For the long night,” he said to me, when he got to me. He said it simply, as if he were offering a cough sweet. “If you like. Totally fine if not.”
“What is it?”

He smiled. “It’s the good one. It’s clean, I’ve checked it. It just makes you kind.” He looked at me over the tops of glasses he was not wearing. “You look like you could do with a few hours of that, friend. No pressure.”
I want to be honest about why I took it, because that is the whole reason I am telling any of this.

I did not take it to feel good. I did not take it because I was curious. I did not even really hear what he said it did. I took it because I wanted, for one night, for a few hours, not to be the man with the envelope in his jacket. I would have taken anything. I would have taken a sugar pill. I wanted to switch myself off the way you switch off a machine that is shaking itself apart on the test bed: the red button, the big one, the one you press when the numbers are going somewhere you cannot follow.
I took one capsule out of the tin. I swallowed it with the last of my wine.
“Drink water, not wine, from now on,” the man said kindly, and moved on round the circle. “Not too much water, either. Sip. And sit down if you get hot.”

I stood by the fire. Nothing happened. The guitar played the same song, badly. The surfer told me about another wave. I thought: nothing. Good. Of course. Nothing ever happens to me. I looked up at the strings of little lights overhead, the net thrown over the garden, and the fig leaves black against them, and a moth going round and round one of the bulbs, and round, and round.
It began in my hands.

I noticed that I was holding the empty glass very lightly, as if it were made of something that might wake. Then I noticed that my hands were warm, all the way through, the way your hands are warm when you have been holding a cup of tea for a long time and have just put it down. Then the warmth was in my arms. Then it was in my chest, and it was not like wine. Wine is a blanket thrown over you. This was something coming up from underneath, like a pilot light being turned up under a cold stove, slowly, steadily, click, click, click, until the whole of me was lit from below.

I looked at the fire. It was the most beautiful fire I had ever seen. Not in a strange way. It did not change shape, or speak, or turn into anything. It was just a fire, a perfectly ordinary fire in a steel pit on Sunny’s cracked patio, and it was the most beautiful fire in the world, and I could not understand why I had never noticed before how beautiful fires were. I could have looked at it for a year.

The surfer was still talking. I listened to him. I really listened. He was telling me about his brother, who had drowned at Point Dume in 1981, and he had been telling me about his brother for some time, it turned out, under the waves, and I had not heard a word of it until now.
“I’m so sorry,” I said. “About your brother.”
He stopped. He looked at me, surprised.
“Thank you, man,” he said, after a moment. “Nobody ever says that. It was forty-five years ago. People think you’re supposed to be over it.”
“You’re not supposed to be over it,” I said. “He was your brother.”
And the old surfer, a man I had known for ten minutes, put his arm round my shoulders, and I put mine round his, and we stood by the fire like that, two strangers, and it was not strange at all.
I have read since, many times, the words other people use for what happened next, and none of them is right, so I will say it plainly.
The fear went.

I had not known it was there. That is the thing I keep coming back to. I had not known that I had been afraid every minute of every day for two years — that there had been a hand on my throat, and a weight in my chest, and a voice at the back of my head saying don’t, don’t, don’t look, don’t say it — until it stopped. It did not fade. It switched off. As if somebody had turned off a machine that had been running in the next room for so long I thought the noise was silence. And in the real silence, after it, I could hear everything.
I could hear myself.

I left the party. I do not remember deciding to; I remember Sunny’s gate under my hand, and the street, and the paper-bark trees standing over it, enormous and silver in the light from the street lamps, peeling, shedding, like old men taking off their shirts. I remember the smell of them, medicine and honey. I remember being warm, so warm, and sitting down on the kerb for a while because the kind bald man had said to sit down if I got hot. And then I was walking up Grand View, past the shut market street, past the dark houses, up the hill, the way I had walked it so many nights, and it was not the same walk. My legs were light. The air was soft as water. Every house I passed, I thought: there are people asleep in there, and they are afraid of something too, and I loved them, all of them, every sleeping stranger, with an ease that frightened me a little, far down, and then didn’t.
At the top I sat down on the kerb at the crest of the hill.

The city fell away below me. The lights went down and down in their orange grid to the place where they stopped, and past them the sea, and tonight the sea was not a hole. There was a moon, almost full, low over the water, and it had laid a long road of light across the black from the horizon almost to the shore, a road you could have walked on, broken and gold and moving.
Mar Vista, I thought. Sea view. It was true tonight. For once the name was telling the truth.

I took out my phone. I opened the little app that records your voice, the one I used at work to dictate notes when my hands were full of test rig. I held it in front of my mouth, the way I held it in the test hall. And I said, in a perfectly ordinary voice, to nobody, to the moon on the water:
“Two million, one hundred and forty thousand dollars.”
I stopped. My heart was going hard, but not with fear. With something I did not have a name for.

“That’s the number,” I said. “I lost it. Me. Mansour’s money, all of it, and the house, there’s a line of credit on the house and I used it and it’s gone. They’re going to sell the house. It’s in my jacket. I’ve never read it to the end. I’m going to read it now.”

I took the envelope out of my jacket and unfolded it, there on the kerb, by the light of my phone, and read it, all of it, to the end, out loud into the phone. Ninety days from the second of April. I counted on my fingers like a child. Ten days left, and after the ten days they would send a date. My voice did not shake.

“I lied to Mina,” I said. “I’ve been lying to her for two years. I lied to her about the money and I lied to her about the line of credit and I made her sign it, I sat at her father’s table and made her sign it, and I told her it was for emergencies. And I lied to Yasi. I bought her a bike with it and I winked.”
I was crying. I noticed that I was crying the way you notice it is raining: oh, there it is. It did not hurt. It came out of me easily, like water out of a spring, and I let it.
“And I lied to me,” I said.

I sat there a long time after that with the phone in my hand, recording nothing, the little red dot going and going. I knew there was more. I could feel it, under the number, the way you can feel through the soles of your feet that the floor of a building is not quite level. There was something underneath the number, bigger than it, and older, and if I sat there long enough, warm and unafraid with the moon on the water, I would hear it.
I did not hear it that night. That night the number was enough. It was the first true thing I had said out loud in two years, and I said it to the sea, and the sea did not mind.

Sunny found me there at three in the morning, sitting on the kerb with my knees up and the phone in my lap. She had come up the hill in her rust-coloured dress and her leafy crown, barefoot on the cold pavement, with a bottle of water. She sat down beside me without a word and gave me the bottle, and I sipped it, the way he had said, and we looked at the moon’s road on the water until it began to fade.
“Did you put it down?” she said at last. “The thing you were carrying?”
“No,” I said. “I picked it up.”
She nodded slowly, as if that were the right answer.
“That’s how it starts, honey,” she said.

The sky went grey over the hills behind us, and then pale, and then the colour of the inside of a shell. The shortest night was over. The year had turned. We walked down the hill together, slowly, in the first light, and the paper-bark trees were shedding their skins over the road, and I was so tired, and somewhere under the tiredness, very small and very far down, like a coal at the bottom of a grate in the morning, there was still that warmth.
At the door of my house I stopped with my key in my hand.

Through the glass of the front door I could see the hall, and the photograph on the wall: the young man in the narrow black suit, squinting into a Los Angeles sun he did not yet trust, outside a shop with a single rug in the window.
I stood there and looked at him. And for the first time in all the years I had lived in his house, I did not look away first.

II. THE NAMING
Eighty-six days.

I slept until noon on the longest day of the year, and woke in my own bed with the sun coming through the glass wall onto the floor in a long bright slab, and Mina sitting on the end of the bed in her robe with two cups of coffee, watching me.
“Look at you,” she said. “Sleeping like a teenager.”
Her headache was gone. Her face was clear and rested, and she was smiling at me with one corner of her mouth, the way she did when she was about to tease. She held out a cup. I sat up and took it.

“Sunny says you were the life of the party,” she said. “She came by at nine with a bowl of figs. She says you and Gary the surfer were hugging.” She drew the word out. “Gary doesn’t hug. Gary hasn’t hugged anyone since 1981.”
“His brother drowned,” I said.
“I know. Everyone knows.”
“Did anyone ever tell him they were sorry?”
She looked at me over her coffee. The teasing went out of her face, slowly, like water going out of sand.
“I don’t know,” she said. “I don’t think so. Not for years.” She tilted her head. “Are you all right?”

I wanted to tell her. I want that to be on the record: on the morning after, sitting up in bed with the coffee in my hands and the sun on the floor, I wanted to tell her more than I have ever wanted anything. It was right there. The whole of it was right there behind my teeth.

But the warmth was gone. That was the thing. In the night it had been under everything like a pilot light, and now it was out, and I could feel exactly where it had been, the way you can feel where a tooth was with your tongue. And in its place the old machine was running again in the next room, humming, humming, don’t, don’t look, don’t say it. Only now I could hear it. That was the difference. Now that I had heard it stop, I could hear it running.
“I’m fine,” I said. “Just tired. Too much wine.”
“You don’t drink too much wine.”
“I did last night.”

She studied me a moment longer. Then she leaned over and kissed my forehead, the way you check a child for fever, and got up and went out to the kitchen, and I sat with the coffee going cold and listened to her moving in the kitchen, the tap, the cupboard, the radio on low, Persian music from the station in Westwood that her father had listened to every morning of his life.

That afternoon, while she was out in the garden with a rug, I went into the garage and shut the door and sat on an old trunk in the dusty half-dark, among the bikes and the Christmas boxes and the cartons of Mansour’s things we had never had the heart to sort, and I played the recording.

It is a strange thing to hear your own voice telling the truth. I had never heard it before. I knew my voice in meetings, in the test hall, reading Yasi stories, saying I’m fine. This was a different man. He spoke slowly. He did not hurry to the end of his sentences the way I do. He paused, and you could hear the night around him, a dog far off, a car going down the hill, the wind. And when he said the number, two million, one hundred and forty thousand dollars, he said it the way you would say the name of a town. Not hiding it. Not dressing it. Just setting it down.

I listened to it three times. The third time, I noticed something I had not noticed the night before. When he said and I lied to me, he stopped, and in the silence after it you could hear him breathe in, as if he were about to go on. As if there were more. And then he didn’t.
I sat in the garage with the phone in my hand, and I thought: what was he going to say?
Eighty-three days.
The low came on the Tuesday.

I did not understand it at first. I woke up on Tuesday morning and the world had gone grey. Not sad, exactly. Flat. As if someone had turned the colour down on everything by a few degrees: the sky over the paper-bark trees, the coffee, Yasi’s face at breakfast telling me about a boy in her chemistry class who had set his own eyebrow on fire. I laughed in the right place. I could not feel the laugh. At work I broke a hinge and wrote it down and could not remember, ten minutes later, what it had carried.
On Wednesday, still grey, I went two doors down after work and knocked on Sunny’s door.
She opened it with clay on her hands to the wrists, grey and wet, and looked at me, and said, “Oh, it’s Tuesday blues. Come in. Wash your hands, you can wedge clay.”
“It’s Wednesday.”

“It always is by the time people come.” She led me through the house, which was dark and cool and full of plants, out to the garage where the kiln was. Her potter’s wheel stood in the middle of the concrete floor, and a long table beside it, and on the table a block of wet grey clay the size of a loaf of bread. “Push that,” she said. “Like dough. Lean on it. Fold it. Push it again. It gets the air out.”

I pushed it. It was cold and heavy and pleasant to push. Sunny sat down at her wheel and set it turning, and put a lump of clay in the middle of it, and wet her hands, and closed them round the clay, and the clay rose up between her hands into a tall wobbling tower, and she pressed it down again, and it rose again.
“You want to know what it was,” she said, without looking up.
“Yes.”

“Leon told you. He just didn’t tell you the name.” The clay rose and fell. “Leon’s a retired pharmacist, by the way. He’s very careful. He tests everything he hands out, and he only hands it out to grown-ups at my house on one night a year, and you’re the first person in about twenty years who took it without asking him a single question.” She glanced up at me. “That was stupid, honey. I want to say that first. Most of what goes around at parties isn’t what people say it is. Some of it now is cut with things that kill you. You got lucky. You were with Leon.”
“I know,” I said. I hadn’t known. I knew now.
“Okay.” She looked back down at her clay. “It was MDMA.”
I stopped pushing.

I knew the letters, of course. Everybody knows the letters. I had heard them on the news my whole life, in stories about raves and teenagers and boys collapsing in fields in England. Ecstasy. Molly. A party drug. A thing for young people with glow sticks. I thought of myself sitting on the kerb at the top of Grand View at one in the morning, saying the number into my phone with tears running down my face, and I could not make the two things fit.
“That’s — ” I said. “I thought that was a party drug.”

“It is now.” Sunny’s hands opened, and the clay was a bowl, suddenly, as if it had been a bowl all along and her hands had only been keeping it secret. “It wasn’t always. You know what we called it, when I first had it? Nineteen eighty-four. I was twenty-eight.” She took her foot off the wheel. The bowl turned slower and slower, and stopped. “We didn’t call it anything with letters. We called it Adam.”
“Adam.”

“Like in the garden. Before the apple.” She wiped her hands on her apron. “Because that’s what it felt like. Like going back to before you knew you were supposed to be ashamed of anything. That’s what the therapists called it. It was the therapists who had it, then, not the kids. They gave it to people in their offices. Married couples. People who’d been through terrible things.” She looked at me. “It was legal, Farzad. Till eighty-five. Nobody had got round to making a law about it.”
“You took it in a therapist’s office?”

“In Santa Monica. On Ocean Park. With my husband.” She smiled, not at me. “We’d been married six years and we hadn’t said one true thing to each other in four of them. We went in at ten in the morning. A woman sat with us all day. We came out at six in the evening and walked down to the beach and sat on the sand and watched the sun go down, and we knew we were going to get divorced, and it was the most loving day of our whole marriage.”
I did not know what to say to that. I wedged the clay. Push, fold, turn, push.

“It doesn’t make you tell the truth,” Sunny said. “People get that wrong. It’s not a truth serum. Nobody holds a gun to your head. It just turns off the part of you that’s afraid of what the truth will cost. That’s all. That’s the whole thing. And you’d be amazed —” she reached over and pressed her thumb into the rim of the new bowl, gently, leaving her mark, “— you would be amazed how much of what we call ourselves is just that one part. Being afraid.”
Eighty days.
At night, in the car, in the parking structure at El Segundo, where I had spent two years watching a line go up and down on a screen, I sat with the engine off and read.
It was the same phone. It was the same seat. My thumb moved the same way on the glass. I noticed that, and it frightened me a little, and I kept reading anyway.

I read that the drug had first been made in 1912, in Germany, in the laboratories of a company called Merck in the city of Darmstadt [DARM-shtaht], by chemists who were not trying to make anything that touched the mind at all. They were working on something to stop bleeding, and it was a step along the way, a chemical on the path to another chemical, and they wrote it down, and patented it, and put it on a shelf, and forgot about it for sixty years. People said for a long time that it had been invented as a diet pill. It had not. That was a story. Even the story of it was a kind of lie.

I read about a chemist in California named Alexander Shulgin [SHUL-gin], who made it again in the 1970s in a small laboratory behind his house in the hills east of San Francisco, and tried it himself, carefully, the way he tried everything, and wrote down what it did. It was not a vision drug, he found. It did not show you anything that was not there. The people who used it after him would call it a window: it let you see out, and see in, and it changed nothing in the room. He gave some to an old friend, a retired psychologist in Oakland named Leo Zeff, who was about to stop working. Zeff tried it and did not stop working. He spent the rest of his life — this is what I read — travelling quietly up and down the country teaching other therapists how to sit with people while they took it, and how to keep them safe, and how to listen. The number of therapists he taught is given in different books as hundreds, or thousands. It was Zeff, I read, who gave it the name Adam.

I read that in 1985 the government made it illegal, in a hurry, after it got out of the therapists’ offices and into the bars of Dallas, and that a judge, after hearing all the doctors who had used it, recommended that it be allowed in medicine anyway, and that the government said no.

I read about the studies that came later, decades later, at last. Soldiers. Firemen. Women who had been through the worst things a person can go through. People who had carried something so heavy for so long that no therapy had ever been able to touch it, who sat in a quiet room for a day with the drug and two kind people, and talked about the thing, and came out, many of them, able to carry it differently. I read that the scientists thought it worked because it turned down the part of the brain that sounds the alarm, the small almond-shaped knot deep in the head that is always listening for danger, while leaving the rest of the mind clear and awake and able to remember everything afterwards. It quiets the fear, as I understood it, so that a person can look directly at the thing they have never been able to look at, and stay.
I read that in 2023 Australia had let psychiatrists prescribe it. I read that in the summer of 2024 the American government had looked at all the studies and said, not yet.

I read the dangers, too. I made myself. That it heats the body, and people at parties have died of the heat. That people have died of drinking too much water, trying not to. That it is hard on the heart. That the low afterwards is real, and comes days later, and can be very dark. That what is sold as it is very often something else. I thought of Leon with his tin and his kind bald head, and of the boys collapsing in fields in England, and of how close a thing it had been.

And I read the word the therapists used, again and again, in the old accounts. Not high. Not trip. They called it a session. As if it were work. As if it were something you sat down to do on purpose, in daylight, with someone beside you, and not something that happened to you by a fire on the shortest night of the year.

I closed the phone. The parking structure was dark and empty and smelled of oil and cold concrete. And I knew, sitting there, the way you know a part is about to fail before the needle moves, that I had to go back. Not to a party. Not by accident. On purpose, to the place where the fear stopped, and sit there, and wait for the thing that was under the number.
I did not know where to begin. I could not ask Leon. I could not ask Sunny for more than she had given me. I was not going to buy something from a stranger in a parking lot.
I went home.

On the first of July the ninety days ran out. Three weeks later, a man I never saw taped a notice to our front door while we were all out, and I found it at six in the evening when I came up the path, a single sheet in a plastic sleeve, with a date on it. The fifteenth of September. Ten o’clock in the morning. The steps of the courthouse in Norwalk.
Fifty-five days.

I took it off the door before anyone else came home. I stood in the hall with it in my hand, under the photograph of Mansour outside his shop, and I did not put it in the drawer. I did not know what to do with it. I could not put it in the drawer and I could not show it to anyone. So I went down the hall and opened the door of the little back bedroom off the garden, Mansour’s room, where nobody went, and stood in it, as if he might tell me.

It was exactly as he had left it, almost four years before. Mina had not been able to clear it. The narrow bed with a rug folded at the foot. The desk under the window. His reading glasses still on the desk, folded, on top of a stack of old auction catalogues. His tweed cap on the hook behind the door. The room smelled of him still, faintly: tea, and wool, and the cologne he had bought at the same shop in Westwood for forty years.
I had come in, I told myself, to look for the deed to the house. I wanted to see it. I wanted to see his name on it, and Mina’s under it, and mine. I opened the drawers of his desk one by one.

The deed was not there. But in the top drawer, under a magnifying glass and a ball of red string and a box of the sugar cubes he took with his tea, there was a small black address book, the old kind, with a soft leather cover worn pale at the corners and a little alphabet cut down the edge of the pages.
I opened it at random. His careful, slanting hand. Rug dealers in Beverly Hills, in Tehran, in Istanbul. A doctor. The lawyer in Encino. The honey man from the market, which made me smile.
I turned to H.
There was only one name under H. Written in blue ink that had faded almost to grey, in a hand younger and quicker than the one I knew, the hand of a man in his thirties.
Dr. M. Hale — Ojai. And a telephone number.
And beside it, in the margin, in Persian script, small, a single word.
Ādam.

— I’m going to tell you a thing I do. A stupid thing.

— At dinner. I say the number. What we have. Out loud, like grace, like a prayer, over the rice. We are worth this much now. Every week, a little more. She’s too small to know what it means. She just knows Baba says the number and smiles.

— (a laugh, not a happy one) It’s there. I’m building it again. Every month I put a little away and I don’t touch it. Not for me. It’s a wall. I’m building a wall around her, brick by brick, so high that nothing can ever come over it. So that she will never, ever have to need anybody.
