III. THE TELLING
Fifty-four days.
I called from the car, in the parking structure at El Segundo, at lunchtime, with the engine off. I had been carrying the address book in my jacket for two days, where the envelope used to be.
It rang and rang. I was about to hang up when someone picked up, and there was a pause, and a woman’s voice said, “Hale.”
Not hello. Just her name. The voice was old, and dry, and very clear, the voice of someone who had spent her life speaking slowly so that frightened people could follow.
“Dr. Hale,” I said. “My name is Farzad Karimi. I’m sorry to bother you. I found your number in my father-in-law’s address book. He passed away. Four years ago. His name was Mansour Sadri.”

There was a silence on the line. Not a long one. Just long enough for me to hear, very faintly, behind her, a wind chime, and a bird, and something that might have been a radio playing in another room.
“I’m sorry for your loss,” she said.

“Thank you. I don’t — I’m not sure why I’m calling. I don’t know how you knew him. I just —” I stopped. My hand was sweating on the phone. “Next to your name he wrote a word. In Persian. It says Adam.”
The silence again.
“Does it,” she said. Not a question.

“I took something,” I said. “Five weeks ago. By accident, more or less. At a party. And I said something out loud that I’ve never been able to say. And there’s more. I know there’s more, under it, and I can’t get to it by myself, and I don’t want to go to a party again, and I don’t —” I heard my own voice, high and fast, the voice of a man selling something. I made myself stop. I made myself breathe. “I’m in trouble,” I said. “My family is. It’s my fault. I want to tell my wife the truth. I have to tell myself first. I don’t know how.”
The bird sang behind her, in Ojai, a hundred miles north.

“Mr. Karimi,” she said. “I’m eighty-two years old. I stopped doing the kind of work you’re thinking of in 1985, when it became a crime, and I’ve never broken that law in forty years. I’m not a dealer. I’m not a guru. I’m a retired family therapist with bad knees and an orange tree.”
“I understand.”
“I don’t think you do.” A pause. “Come on Saturday. Not this one, the next. Come at eight in the morning. Bring nothing. Don’t eat breakfast. Tell your wife where you are.”
The line went dead.
I sat in the car with the phone in my lap. Tell your wife where you are.

That night at dinner I told Mina there was a work thing the Saturday after next, an offsite, a team day up the coast in Santa Barbara, all day, and I would be home late. She said, “On a Saturday? They’re working you to death,” and passed me the rice.
It was the last lie. I knew it was the last one as I told it. That did not make it any smaller.
Forty-five days.

You leave Los Angeles in the dark, if you are going to Ojai for eight. Up the 405 empty and grey, over the pass and into the Valley, then the 101 north and west, through the long dry hills of the Conejo where the oaks stand alone on the brown slopes like cattle, and down at last, as the sun comes up behind you, to the sea at Ventura, where the road runs along the edge of the water for a mile and the surfers are already out, black dots on the grey. Then you leave the sea and turn inland, up a narrow valley, on a two-lane road that follows a dry riverbed between walls of rock and scrub, and the air changes. It gets warmer, and drier, and it smells of sage and dust and, as you come up out of the gorge into the open, oranges.

Ojai sits in a bowl. That is the first thing you understand about it. A small round valley, flat and green, all orchards and oak trees and low wooden houses, with mountains on every side, and to the east, standing over the whole valley like a wall, a long high ridge of bare rock that the people there call the Topa Topa [TOH-puh TOH-puh]. I had heard of the town all my life, the way everybody in Los Angeles has: the place the hippies went in the sixties, and the spiritual teachers before that, and the rich people after. A little main street with a long white arcade of Spanish arches, shops selling crystals and expensive soap. An open-air bookshop where the shelves stand outside under the trees and you leave your money in a box in the wall if nobody is there. It looked, that early in the morning, like a town in a children’s book, too clean and too quiet to be real.

Her house was on the east side of the valley, at the end of a dirt road through an orange grove, an old wooden ranch house painted the colour of cream gone slightly yellow, with a deep porch and a tin roof and a wind chime made of old keys. An old dog lay on the porch and lifted its head when I got out of the car and put it down again.
She was waiting in the doorway.

I had imagined someone like Sunny, I realise now. Braids, bare feet, silver rings. Margaret Hale was a small straight old woman in a grey cardigan buttoned to the neck and a pair of sensible brown shoes, with white hair cut short as a boy’s, and reading glasses on a cord, and pale grey eyes that took me in from head to foot in one look, the way a doctor looks at a man coming through the door before he says a word.
“You didn’t eat,” she said.
“No.”

“Good. Come in. We’re going to sit in the kitchen first and you’re going to answer my questions, and if I don’t like the answers you’re going to drive home, and I’ll make you a sandwich for the road.”

The kitchen was yellow and old and full of morning light. There was a big scrubbed wooden table with a bowl of oranges on it, and a kettle on the stove, and on the wall a calendar from a feed store in town with a photograph of a horse. She sat me at the table and sat down opposite me and put on her reading glasses and took out a pad of paper and a pen, and for an hour she asked me questions.

They were not the questions I expected. She asked about my heart. My blood pressure. Every medicine I took, and every one I had taken in the last six months, and she wrote them all down, and when I mentioned a pill I had taken for a while for sleep, two years ago, she asked me exactly when I had stopped, and looked at me over her glasses until she was satisfied. She asked if anyone in my family had ever been ill in their mind. She asked whether I had ever heard voices, or been unable to sleep for days and felt wonderful. She asked about the party, and what the capsule had looked like, and how I had felt the days after, and she nodded when I told her about the Tuesday. She asked if I had thought, in the last months, of hurting myself.
I said no. Then I thought about the top of the hill at night, and the place where the lights stopped, and the way I used to stand and look at it.
“I don’t think so,” I said. “I used to walk up a hill and look at the dark. I never thought of — I just looked.”
She looked at me over her glasses without a word. Then she wrote something down, and underlined it.
“If that changes,” she said, “you tell me, or you tell your doctor, or you call 988, which is the number now, and you do it that same hour. Not the next day. Do you understand me?”
“Yes.”
“Say it.”
“If it changes, I tell someone the same hour.”
“Good.” She put the pen down. “Now I’m going to tell you some things, and then you’re going to decide.”

She told me what I had read in the car, but she told it differently, because she had been there. She told me about Leo Zeff, whom she had met in 1979, a small bald man with a gentle voice who had been a psychologist all his life and who, in his sixties, she said, had started again. She told me how he had taught her to sit with people. “The medicine is the least of it,” she said. “That’s what I took from Leo, anyway. It’s maybe ten percent. The rest is who you are when you come in, and where you are, and who’s sitting with you. A frightened man in a loud room with strangers gets a frightened night. A man who has come on purpose, on an empty stomach, to a quiet room, with someone who is not going anywhere — that man gets something else. It’s the same molecule. It’s not the same day.”

She told me what she would do. I would lie on a couch in the next room. She would sit in a chair beside me, all day, and she would not leave. There would be music if I wanted it and silence if I didn’t. She would ask very few questions. She would not tell me what to think. “I’m not going to dig,” she said. “I’m not a dentist. Whatever comes up comes up by itself. My job is to keep you safe and keep you company while it does.”

She told me the dangers, plainly, in a list, the way I would have written them down myself. The heat. The water. The heart. The low that comes days later. That it was not magic. That some people came out of a day like this with nothing, and some came out worse, carrying a thing they had found and could not put down. That afterwards, the work was mine to do, in my own life, with my own family, without anything in my blood at all. “This is a day,” she said. “It’s one day. It’s not a cure. It doesn’t fix anything. It just turns the lights on in a room you’ve been walking round in the dark, and you see where the furniture is. You still have to move it yourself.”
And she told me the last thing, which was that what she was about to do was against the law, and that she had decided to do it, once, and that she would not tell me why.
“Is it because of Mansour?” I said.
She took her glasses off and folded them and put them down on the pad, on top of the line she had underlined.
“I said I wouldn’t tell you why,” she said. “Do you want to go home, Mr. Karimi, or do you want to lie down?”
The room was at the back of the house, facing east.

It was very plain. A long low couch made up with clean white sheets and a heavy grey blanket. A wooden chair beside it with a cushion. A small table with a jug of water and a glass, and a box of tissues, and a clock that ticked. A window that looked out over the orange trees to the long bare wall of the Topa Topa, gold now in the morning sun. And on the floor, between the couch and the chair, a small old rug.

I noticed it because I notice rugs. You cannot live with Mina for twenty-four years and not notice rugs. It was a Kashan, a very good one, old, the reds gone soft as wine and the blues gone almost to grey, a garden pattern, with a vase in the middle and flowers coming out of it in every direction. Someone had mended one corner, beautifully, so that you could hardly see it.
“That’s a fine rug,” I said.

“It was a gift,” Dr. Hale said. “From a grateful man. A long time ago.” She held out her hand. In her palm was a single capsule, the colour of sand, exactly like the one from Leon’s tin. She did not tell me where it had come from and I did not ask. “It is what it is,” she said. “I’ve made sure of that. Lie down when you’ve taken it. Put the blanket over you. People get cold at the start, and then warm.”

I took it with a glass of water at a quarter past nine. I lay down on the couch and pulled the grey blanket up to my chest. Dr. Hale sat down in the wooden chair beside me, and folded her hands in her lap, and looked out of the window at the mountain, and said nothing at all.
The clock ticked. A bird sang in the orange trees. The old dog came in and lay down on the rug, on the garden pattern, with a long sigh.
I waited, and nothing happened, and I was afraid that nothing would.

And then, at about ten o’clock, it came the way it had come by Sunny’s fire, in my hands first, a warmth like holding a glass of tea. Up my arms. Into my chest. The pilot light under the cold stove, click, click, click. And then, the way it had before, the humming in the next room stopped.

But it was not like the party. That was the first thing I understood. At the party I had been loud inside, glad and loose and loving everyone, a man let out of a box. Here, in the quiet room, with the old woman in the chair and the mountain in the window, it was not loud at all. It was very, very still. As if I had been let out of the box into a church.
“Mr. Karimi,” she said, after a long time. Her voice was soft and came from very close. “Where are you?”
“Here,” I said. And then, because it was true, “I’m not afraid.”
“Good. You don’t have to do anything. Just be there.”
So I was there.

I lay under the grey blanket in the sun and I thought about nothing for a long time. I thought about the rug. I thought about the hands that had mended its corner, so carefully, and I thought that was the most beautiful thing a person could do, to take something torn and make it whole and not even leave a mark, and I cried a little about that, easily, and Dr. Hale passed me a tissue without looking, and I laughed, and she smiled at the mountain.
Then, after a while, without deciding to, I began to talk.

I told her the number. It came out of me as easily as it had on the hill, and more easily, the way a word comes easier the second time you say it in a new language. Two million, one hundred and forty thousand dollars. I told her about the boy at the next bench and the burst of light. The bathroom. The car. The Monday in August when the world sold. The line of credit, and Mina’s small upright signature, and the lemon flowers. The drawer. The notice on the door. The fifteenth of September.
I told her all of it, in order, like a report. Like the report of a test. Load applied. Point of failure. Cause. And when I had finished, I lay there, warm and unafraid, and waited to feel lighter.
“Why?” said Dr. Hale.
“Why what?”
“Why did you keep going?”

“To win it back,” I said. “For them. For Mina and Yasi. I’d lost it, so I had to get it back before anyone knew. I wanted to give it back to them. Every time I lost I thought, one more, and I can give it back. That’s why. I wanted to look after them. He asked me to.”
She didn’t say anything. The clock ticked.
“Is that true?” she said.
I want to tell this part slowly. It happened slowly, and it is the part of my life I understand least and believe most.

Her question was not unkind. It was not an accusation. She asked it the way you would ask someone is the window open? — as if it were simply a thing that might be one way or the other, and she would like to know. And I lay there with it, under the blanket, and I started to say yes, and I could not.

Not because anything stopped me. Because there was nothing to stop. Every other time in my life when somebody had asked me a question like that, there had been a hand on my throat, and the hand had always helped me: it had put the right answer in my mouth, quickly, before I had to look at the real one. Yes, of course. For them. The hand was gone. And without it, the answer just sat there, and I looked at it, and it was not true.

It was not not true. I had wanted to win it back. I had wanted to give it to them. But under that — I could feel it, the way I had felt it on the hill, the floor of the building not quite level — under that there was something else, and now that the fear was gone, I could not stop myself from looking at it.
“No,” I said. “It’s not — not all.”
“All right.”
I lay there. The sun had moved and was on my hands now, on the grey blanket.

I thought about the burst of light. I thought about how it had felt, the first time, in the toilet stall in El Segundo. I had always remembered it as joy. Being right. Lifting the heavy world with a small push on a long lever. And I lay in the warm still room and I made myself remember it again, honestly, the way you play back a test on slow motion to see the exact moment the crack starts. And I saw that the joy had not been about the money. It had not been about Mina or Yasi. It had been about me. For the first time in fifteen years there was something in that house that I had done. Not Mansour. Me.
“I lived in his house,” I said.
“Yes.”

“Fifteen years. His house. His name on the door. His photograph in the hall. His rugs on the floor. His lemon tree. He paid the tax, he wouldn’t let me. He slept in the little room at the back because he wouldn’t take the big one, and every night I lay in the big one and I knew it was his, he was giving it to me, every single night he was giving me my own bed.” My voice was very quiet. It did not shake. “I loved him. I want you to know that. I loved him. He was the most generous man I ever met. And I was a guest. Every day. Every single day for fifteen years I was a guest in another man’s house, and I was so grateful, and I was so ashamed, and I never told anybody, I never even told myself, because what kind of man is ashamed of a gift?”
Dr. Hale said nothing. The old dog breathed on the rug.
“And then he died,” I said, “and he gave me the money too.”
I stopped. Something was coming up from very far down. I could feel it the way you feel a train in the rails before you hear it.

“Look after it anyway,” I said. “That’s what he wrote. She will tell you she does not need you to look after the money. She will be right. Look after it anyway. The last thing he ever said to me. And I thought it was — I thought he was trusting me. Finally. After all those years. And I was so happy. And I went into the garden that night after the lawyer left and I stood under his lemon tree and I —”
I stopped again. I could not believe what I was about to say. And I was not afraid of it. That was the strangest thing. I was not afraid of it at all.
“I hated him,” I said.
The words lay in the room. Plain, ordinary. Like the name of a town.

“Not him,” I said. “Not really. I hated being given. I hated that he’d built a wall around her so high that nobody could ever come over it, and I lived inside the wall, and the wall was made of money, his money, and even when he was dead he’d left me one more brick to carry. Look after it. His money. In his house. So she’d never need anybody. Never need me.” I was crying now, but it did not hurt. It came out of me like water. “And every time I lost — every time the number went down —”
I could not say it. Then I could.
“I felt lighter,” I said.
I heard Dr. Hale let out a breath, very softly, beside me.

“Every time,” I said. “God help me. Every time I lost, there was this — this little bit of relief, under the fear, so small I never let myself see it. A brick coming off the wall. When the zero came up that Monday in August, that little grey polite zero, I sat in the car and I was sick with terror and I was — I was glad. I was so glad. Because it was less of him. Every dollar I lost was a dollar of his that wasn’t standing between me and my own wife. I wasn’t trying to win it back. I never was. I was trying to get rid of it. I was trying to knock down his wall with my bare hands so there’d be something left that was mine.”
The room was very quiet.
“I didn’t lose the money,” I said. “I threw it away. And I told myself I was trying to save it, every single day, for two years, and I believed it. I believed it until about a minute ago.”
I lay there and looked at what I had said, and it was terrible, and it was true, and it was the first time in my whole life I had seen the bottom of anything.
And then — I do not know how else to put this — I grieved him.

For four years I had not. I had held Mina on the kitchen floor. I had stood at the grave. I had carried the coffin. But I had not grieved him, because you cannot grieve a man while you are still standing inside his wall pretending to be grateful for it. And now, in the warm, still room, with the hand off my throat, I could. All of it came at once. The tweed cap. The blue eggs he bought because they were beautiful. Sunny jān. The shutter going up every morning at nine with the line of Rumi. Ask me when you are older. The young man in the narrow black suit squinting into a sun he didn’t trust. I had loved him and feared him and envied him and hated him and owed him everything, and he was dead, and I would never be able to tell him any of it.

I wept until there was nothing left to weep with. Dr. Hale sat beside me and did not touch me and did not speak, and the clock ticked, and the sun went slowly across the floor and over the old rug and up the wall.
At some point I heard her say, very quietly, almost to herself, “There it is.”
Still forty-five days.

The warmth went slowly, in the afternoon, the way the sun goes off a wall. By four o’clock I was sitting up on the couch with a glass of water and a plate of sliced oranges from her trees, which were the best oranges I had ever eaten, and I said so, and she said everyone said so, it was the medicine and the oranges both, and it was not worth separating them. By five I could stand. By six she let me go out on the porch, and we sat side by side in two old wooden chairs, with the dog between us, and looked at the mountain.
Then the thing happened that the people of that valley call the pink moment.

The sun was going down behind us, over the western hills, and as it went, the long bare face of the Topa Topa in front of us, which had been gold all day, began to change. It went amber. Then rose. Then a deep, glowing, impossible pink, the whole mountain at once, as if it were lit from inside, as if the rock itself had blushed. It lasted about five minutes. Nobody on the porch said anything. And then it was over, and the mountain was grey-blue and ordinary, and the first star came out above it.
“Every evening,” Dr. Hale said. “Forty years I’ve watched it. It’s never once been the same.”
We sat in the dusk. The wind chime of old keys moved and clinked.
“What do I do now?” I said.

“Now you know what’s yours,” she said. “You can’t hand somebody a truth you haven’t held. Not your wife. Not your daughter. You’d only be handing them the version you could stand to say, and they’d know. They always know.” She looked at me sideways, in the half-dark. “You’ve held it now. You can’t un-know it. That’s the gift and that’s the cost, both.”
“I have to tell her.”
“Yes.”

“All of it. The money. The line of credit. That I —” I could not finish. Without the warmth in me, the old hum had come back, and I could hear it again, in the next room. Don’t. Don’t say it. But it was quieter now. It sounded like a machine somebody had forgotten to turn off, not a voice that knew things.
“Bring her,” said Dr. Hale.
I looked at her.

“If she’ll come,” she said. “If she wants to. Not to fix anything. Not to be told. Bring her and let her sit where you sat today, and you sit in the chair, and you see what she has to say. You might be surprised.” She paused. “People who live inside walls aren’t usually the only ones who know they’re there.”
I did not understand her. I thought I did. I thought she meant that Mina would be angry, or hurt, or that she would forgive me. I did not understand at all.
“Why are you doing this?” I said. “You said you’d never broken the law in forty years.”
She did not answer at first. The dog sighed and rolled over on the boards.
“Your father-in-law sang,” she said at last. “Didn’t he? When he was nervous.”
I turned and stared at her.

“Drive home carefully, Mr. Karimi,” she said, and stood up, slowly, with a hand on the arm of her chair. “Eat something before the highway. And tell your wife where you were today. Tonight. Before you go to sleep.”

I drove down out of the valley in the dark, through the gorge, and the oranges gave way to sage and the sage to the smell of the sea, and at Ventura the road ran along the water again, black now, with the lights of the oil platforms out on it like small burning cities. I drove the whole way home without the radio. I did not think of anything. I held the wheel and watched the road come up white in the headlights.
At the house all the lights were off except one, in the kitchen.
Mina was sitting at the dining table, in the dark, in her robe, in her father’s place. In front of her, on the table, laid out flat and neat in a row, were three things.
The Notice of Default, from under the takeout menus.
The notice of sale, with the date on it, the one I had taken off the front door and hidden in the inside pocket of my winter coat.
And her own phone, face up, the screen lit, showing the login page of the account her father had left her.
She looked up at me as I stood in the doorway with the car keys still in my hand.
“How was Santa Barbara?” she said.

IV. THE ROOM
Still forty-five days.

I put the car keys down on the counter. I did not sit. I stood at the end of the table, by the glass wall, with the black garden behind me and my own reflection hanging in it like a man standing outside in the dark, looking in.
“I wasn’t in Santa Barbara,” I said.
“I know.”
“I was in Ojai.”
That was the first time I saw her face move. A small thing, around the eyes, as if somebody had touched a bruise.
“Ojai,” she said.
“I’ll tell you. I’ll tell you all of it. Can I tell you the money first?”

She looked at me. Then she pushed the chair beside her out from the table with her foot, a few inches, the way you might make room on a bench. I sat down in it. And there, at her father’s table, at eleven at night, with nothing in my blood but coffee from a gas station in Ventura, I told her.

It was not like Ojai, and you should know that. It was not like the hill. The hum was there, in the next room, the whole time, louder than it had been all day. Don’t. Don’t say it. Not like this. My throat kept closing. Twice I had to stop and put my hands flat on the table and breathe, and wait for it to open. But I knew now what the hum was. It was not a voice that knew things. It was a machine somebody had left running. And you can talk over a machine. You just have to talk louder.

I told her the number. I told her about the boy at the bench, and the bathroom, and the Monday in August. I told her about the line of credit, and the lemon flowers, and that I had sat in this chair and watched her sign it and called it emergencies. I told her about the drawer, and the menus, and the hill at night, and the place where the lights stopped. I told her about Sunny’s fire and Leon’s tin and the moon on the water. I told her about the address book.
When I said Hale, she closed her eyes.

And then I told her the last part. The part from the couch in Ojai. That I had not been trying to win it back. That every time it fell, I had felt lighter. That I had been knocking her father’s wall down with my bare hands, a brick at a time, because I could not bear to live inside it any more, and I had told myself the whole time that I was trying to save it.

I said it without the warmth. Without anything. It was the hardest thing I have ever said, harder than the number, harder than anything, and I said it to her face, and my voice broke in the middle of it and I went on anyway.
When I had finished, the kitchen was very quiet. The fridge hummed. Somewhere down the hall Yasi’s music was playing very softly through her door.
Mina had not cried. She had not moved, the whole time, except once, when I told her about the wall. She was looking at the account login on her phone, lit on the table between us.
“I want to say something to you,” she said at last. Her voice was very calm. Too calm. “And I can’t.”
“Mina —”

“Not won’t. Can’t.” She touched her own throat with two fingers, lightly, as if she were checking for something there. “It’s right here. And it won’t come out. Not with my face. Not in this kitchen.” She looked up at me. Her eyes were dry and enormous. “Take me to her.”
“You don’t have to —”

“He went every April,” she said. “Every April of my whole life. To see an old friend. And I never once asked him who.” She stood up. She picked up the two notices and folded them together, neatly, in three, the way I had folded every letter, and the way her father had folded his. “Take me to her, Farzad. I want to see who he went to see.”
We told Yasi on Sunday morning, at the market.

It was Mina’s idea. Not in the house, she said. Not at the table. Somewhere with people in it. So we walked up to Grand View, the three of us, the way we had every Sunday for fifteen years, and bought coffee, and stood at the end of the street by Sunny’s stall of river-coloured bowls, and I told my daughter that we were going to lose the house, and that it was my fault, and why.

Not all of it. The parts a girl of nearly fifteen needs. That I had made bad bets with Baba’s money, and kept making them, and hidden them, and that on the fifteenth of September the bank would sell the house, and we would have to move.
She listened with her hands wrapped round her cup. She was taller than her mother now. She looked at me with Mansour’s eyes, heavy-lidded and dark, and I could not tell what she was thinking.
“Is that why you were weird?” she said. “For, like, two years?”
“Yes.”
“Okay.” She looked into her cup. “I thought you were getting divorced.”
Mina made a small sound.
“I thought it was me,” Yasi said, very quietly, to the coffee. “I thought you didn’t like being home because of me.”

I put my arms round her, there, in the middle of the market, with her coffee squashed between us and spilling on my shirt, and she let me, for a long time, longer than she had let me hold her since she was eleven.
“Noor lives in an apartment in Palms,” she said into my chest, at last, muffled. “It has a pool. A rooftop pool.”
“Does it,” I said.

“It’s not even that far. I could still bike to school.” She pulled back and wiped her nose on her sleeve and looked at me fiercely, the way her grandfather used to look at a rug. “Don’t do it again. The weird thing. The hiding thing. If something’s bad, just say it’s bad.”
“I promise.”

“Okay.” She drank her coffee. Then she looked past me at the honey stall, where the man was setting out his jars with the names of the hills on them. “Baba used to say the sage one was the best,” she said. “Grandpa, I mean. He was wrong. It’s the orange blossom.” And she walked off to argue with the honey man, and Mina and I stood among the bowls and held on to each other, and Sunny, behind her table, very carefully did not look at us at all.
Thirty-one days.

We drove up on a Saturday in the middle of August, in the dark, the way I had before. Mina did not speak the whole way to Ventura. She sat with her hands in her lap, looking out of the window at the black hills of the Conejo going by, and when the sun came up behind us and we came down to the sea, she said, “He’d have stopped here. For tea. He always stopped for tea,” and I pulled into the lot by the pier, and we sat in the car with two paper cups from the gas station and watched the surfers, and she still did not speak.
Up the gorge. The sage. The oranges. The bowl of the valley green and quiet in the early light, and the Topa Topa standing over it gold.
Dr. Hale was waiting in the doorway, in her grey cardigan, with the old dog at her feet.

Mina got out of the car and stood on the dirt, by the orange trees, and looked at her. And the old woman looked back. For a long moment neither of them said anything at all. Then Dr. Hale came down the porch steps, slowly, with one hand on the rail, and crossed the yard, and stopped in front of my wife, and looked up into her face.
“You have his eyes,” she said.
“You knew him.”
“Yes.”
“How?” Mina’s voice was perfectly steady. “How did you know my father?”

“I’ll tell you,” Dr. Hale said. “I’ll tell you anything you want to know. But not out here, and not yet. Come inside and let me ask you my questions first. And then, afterwards, if you still want to, you can ask me yours.” She held out her hand. “My name is Margaret.”
Mina looked at the hand. Then she took it.

The kitchen. The yellow light, the oranges, the feed-store horse on the wall. Dr. Hale asked Mina every question she had asked me, and some I had not heard, and wrote everything down, and underlined things, and twice looked at Mina over her glasses without speaking. She asked about the headaches. She asked about the pills for them, every one, and when Mina had last taken them, and made her say the date. She asked if Mina wanted me in the room.
Mina turned and looked at me, across the kitchen table.
“Yes,” she said. “I want him to hear.”

So it was me in the wooden chair, that day. Dr. Hale brought a second one from the kitchen and sat in it, a little behind me, where Mina could see her without turning her head. And Mina lay on the long low couch under the grey blanket, with the mountain in the window, and took the capsule from the old woman’s palm at a quarter past nine, with a glass of water, and lay back, and closed her eyes.
Then she opened them again and turned her head on the pillow and looked down at the floor, at the small rug between the couch and the chairs.
She sat up.
“Mina?”

She did not answer me. She got off the couch and knelt on the floor in her socks, and put out her hand, and turned back the corner of the rug, the corner with the mend in it, and held it up to the light from the window.
The thread was the colour of pomegranate seeds.
“That’s mine,” she said.
I did not understand. I looked at Dr. Hale. The old woman’s face had gone very still.

“That’s my thread,” Mina said. “That’s my stitch. I did that. At home. In the garden. He brought it home in February, the last winter, rolled up under his arm, and he said it was for a friend, and he asked me to make it so nobody would know, and I did, and he took it away in April and I never —” Her voice cracked. “I never asked him. I never asked him who it was for.”

“He gave me that rug in the spring of 1985,” Dr. Hale said quietly. “It was the best rug he had then, the one he would never sell, and he gave it to me, and I tried to refuse it, and he wouldn’t let me. A cat got at the corner, six winters ago. I told him about it on the porch the next April, just in passing. I didn’t ask him to do anything.” She looked at the corner in Mina’s hand. “He brought it back the April after that. Mended. It was the last time he came. He wouldn’t say who’d done it. He just sat on the porch and watched the mountain and smiled.”

Mina knelt on the floor of that room with the corner of her father’s rug in her hand, and her own stitches in the corner, and began, at last, for the first time since the kitchen floor four years before, to cry.
Dr. Hale got up. She came round the chairs, slowly, with her bad knees, and she put one hand on Mina’s back, between the shoulder blades, and left it there.
“Lie down, honey,” she said. “Lie down now. It’s coming. Let it come.”

It took a long time. Longer than it had for me. She lay under the grey blanket for an hour and more with her face to the window and her eyes open, and said nothing, and I sat in the wooden chair and watched the light move across the floor, across the rug, across her mended corner, and I was more afraid than I had been on any day of the whole two years.
At half past ten, without turning her head, she said, “Farzad.”
“I’m here.”
“I’m so warm.”
“I know.”
“Is this what it was? On the hill?”
“Yes.”
“Oh,” she said, very softly, and then she laughed, a small cracked surprised laugh, like someone opening a door they had thought was locked. “Oh. It’s quiet.”
And then she said it. Quite simply. Still looking at the mountain.
“I knew.”
The clock ticked.

“From the second month,” she said. “I want you to know that. Not the end. Not the letters. The second month. I said I didn’t want to look at it. I said it to your face, at the table, the night the lawyer came, and I meant it when I said it, and I looked at it the next Sunday. After the market. While you were in the shower. And every Sunday after. I watched you do everything right, that first year. And then I watched the first five thousand go into that app, and by the second month I knew. Two years, Farzad. I saw every trade you made. I sat in the bathroom at home on a Sunday morning and looked at the number while you sat in the bathroom at work and looked at the same one.”
I could not speak.

“I watched you buy the bike,” she said. “I knew where the money came from. I watched the Monday in August. I sat in the garden with a rug in my lap and watched it go to zero, and I didn’t call you, and I didn’t say anything when you came home, and I made dinner.” She was crying, now, quietly, but her voice did not stop. “I read the line of credit. Every page. I always read everything. I knew exactly what it was for. And I signed it.”
“Why?” I said. It came out of me like a breath. “Mina. Why?”
She turned her head on the pillow, then, and looked at me. Her face was wet and open and younger than I had seen it in years.
“Because every time it went down,” she said, “I could breathe.”
The room was silent.

“I grew up inside that number,” she said. “Do you understand? It was the walls of my bedroom. He said it at dinner. He said it at my mother’s — he said it when I was sick, when I was sad, when I wanted to go to college in New York, when I wanted to marry you. We are worth this much. You will never need anyone. It wasn’t a promise, Farzad. It was a sentence. I have never needed anyone in my life. I have never let myself. Not him. Not my friends. Not you. I married you and I loved you and I never once, not once in twenty-four years, needed you, because he’d made sure I’d never have to. And when he died, and that money came to me, I thought — I sat at that table with that lawyer and I thought, now I’m going to be inside it forever.” Her breath shook. “And then you started losing it. And it was the worst thing that had ever happened to us. And every Sunday I looked at the number and it was smaller and I felt — I felt like a window was opening. A crack. Air coming in.” She closed her eyes. “I let you do it. I wanted you to do it. I wanted it gone as much as you did. I just wanted you to be the one who did it, so I wouldn’t have to be.”
Dr. Hale, behind me, did not move.

“We were lying to each other,” Mina said, “about the same thing. For two years. In the same house. Both of us praying for the same wall to fall down and both of us pretending we were trying to hold it up.”

I got out of the chair. I knelt on the floor beside the couch, on her father’s rug, on her own mended corner, and put my forehead against her arm on the blanket, and we stayed like that, the two of us, while the clock ticked.

“I need you,” she said into my hair, at last. Clumsily. Like a word in a language she was only beginning. “I need you, Farzad. There. I said it. I’ve never said it to anyone.” She laughed again, wet and amazed. “It’s so easy. Why was it so hard?”
In the afternoon, when the warmth was going off her the way the sun goes off a wall, she sat up on the couch with a plate of sliced oranges and looked at Dr. Hale.
“Now,” she said. “Tell me.”
So Margaret Hale told us.

In the spring of 1985, she said, a man had come to her office in Santa Monica — she had an office then, on Ocean Park; she moved up to the valley the year after — a Persian man in a narrow black suit, thirty-five years old, very polite, very proud, who had heard about her from another Iranian in the rug trade. He had sat in the waiting room for twenty minutes without speaking. When she called him in, he had stood in the doorway and said, before he even sat down, I have lost everything twice, and I have a daughter of three, and I am frightened every minute of my life, and I have never said that sentence to any person. And then he had sat down and said, I would like to try your medicine, please.

“He sat with me one day,” she said. “One day. It was legal for another few weeks. He talked for six hours. Before we began he asked me to record it, on a little machine I had, from the moment the warmth came, so he could take it home and keep it. One side of one tape. I turned it over when it ran out and he said no, that was enough, leave the other side.” She looked at Mina. “I never knew what he did with it. I asked him, once, years later. He just smiled.”
“And every April —” said Mina.

“Every April for thirty-seven years he came up the gorge and sat on my porch for a day and watched the mountain go pink.” The old woman smiled, very slightly. “We hardly talked. Sometimes not at all. He’d bring a bag of oranges from the market in Los Angeles, which is ridiculous, because I live in an orange grove. And at the end of the day he’d stand up and say, Thank you, Margaret, for keeping it, and drive home.” She was quiet a moment. “I always thought he meant the tape. I don’t think he did. I think he meant the day. That one day. I think I was the only person in the world who’d ever seen him without the wall.”
Ocean Park, I thought, and thought of Sunny, in 1984, with her husband, and a woman sat with us all day. I did not say it. I have never asked either of them.
Mina sat with the plate of oranges in her lap and did not eat them.

“When you rang,” Dr. Hale said, turning to me, “and you said his name, and then you said Adam, I knew whose son-in-law you were. I’d heard about you. Every April. My daughter has married an engineer. A careful man. He breaks things to find out how strong they are.” She took off her glasses. “And then you said you’d lost it all. And you wanted to tell your wife. And I thought — I sat in my kitchen with the phone in my hand, and I thought, oh, Mansour. Oh, my dear. It’s happening again.”
“Is that why you said yes?”

“I said yes,” said Margaret Hale, “because forty years ago a frightened man sat on my couch and asked me to keep something for him. And I never knew what it was. And I wanted, before I die, to find out.”
Twenty-eight days.

The low came for Mina on the Tuesday, as it had for me, and it was worse. She lay in our bed in the dark for most of a day, flat and grey, and I sat with her, and brought her water and toast she didn’t eat, and Yasi came and lay down on the bed on the other side of her, in her shoes, with her headphones on, and the three of us lay there in the afternoon like people waiting out a storm.
“It’s not the medicine,” Mina said once, into the pillow. “Not only. It’s him. I’m missing him. I didn’t miss him before. I didn’t let myself.”
“I know.”
“Four years late.”
“I know,” I said. “Me too.”
On the Wednesday she got up. On the Thursday we started to pack.

You do not know how much a family owns until you have to put it in boxes. Fifteen years in that house, and twenty-five before that of Mansour’s alone, and every cupboard opened onto another cupboard. Sunny came every evening after the market closed and wrapped glass in newspaper with her clay-cracked hands and told us stories about the people who had lived on our street before us. Gary the surfer came with a truck and did not speak much and carried the heavy things, the dresser, the dining table, Mansour’s desk, and once, carrying a box of Yasi’s old toys down the path, he stopped and put it down and stood on the lawn with his hand over his eyes for a while, and then picked it up again, and nobody said anything about it, because everybody on that street knew about his brother.

We found an apartment in Palms. Not Noor’s building. Smaller. Two bedrooms over a dry cleaner’s on Venice Boulevard, a mile east of the house, with a balcony that looked at the back of a supermarket and, if you leaned out a long way and turned your head, a sliver of the hills. There was no pool. Yasi said she did not care about the pool. She said it very loudly, twice.

The rugs went to a dealer in Beverly Hills, all but three. The good furniture went. My car went. The kind small tidy lawyer from Encino came round one evening and sat at our dining table one last time, in Mansour’s place, and drank the tea this time, and told us gently which things the bank could take and which it couldn’t, and at the door he shook my hand and held it a moment and said, “He would have forgiven you, you know. He’d have been angry for a week. And then he’d have forgiven you,” and I said, “I know,” and found that I did.
Mansour’s room, and the garage, we left until last.
Nine days.

The garage was the very last of it. Mansour’s cartons were stacked against the back wall, behind the bikes and the Christmas boxes, where we had put them four years before and not been able to look at them since. Six cardboard boxes, taped shut, labelled in his careful hand in Persian and English. Shop papers. Books. Winter clothes. We opened them on a Sunday night, Mina and I, sitting on the concrete floor under the one bare bulb, with Yasi asleep in the house.
The fourth box said Music.

Inside were cassettes. Dozens of them, in their little plastic cases, the old Persian singers he had listened to in the car before cars stopped having cassette players. The great voices: Banan [bah-NAHN]. Marzieh [mar-zee-YEH]. Shajarian [shah-jah-ree-AHN], young. A tape of the Westwood radio station recorded off the air, with the advertisements still on it. Mina took them out one by one and laid them on the floor and read the names out softly, and some of them she remembered, and some of them made her laugh.
At the bottom of the box, under all of them, there was one more.

It was not in a case. It was wrapped in a folded handkerchief, white, with a blue thread border, and inside the handkerchief was a plain grey cassette with a paper label, and on the label, in faded blue ink, in the young, quick hand from the address book:
Ādam. Ojai. 1364. The year in the Persian calendar that runs from the spring of 1985.
Mina held it in both hands, in the handkerchief, and did not open it any further.

We had nothing to play it on. Nobody does now. It was past ten on a Sunday night. And I said, tomorrow, I’ll find something tomorrow, and she said, “No. Tonight,” and I did not argue. I went up the street to Sunny’s, and knocked, and Sunny opened the door in a long nightdress with her grey braid over her shoulder, and listened, and went into her back room without a word, and came back with a big old silver radio-and-tape player the size of a suitcase, with two round speakers, the kind boys used to carry on their shoulders on the boardwalk in Venice when Sunny was young.
“It still works,” she said. “Batteries are new. Go on.”

We sat at the dining table. It was the last night the table would be in the house; Gary was coming for it in the morning. The house around us was almost empty, the walls bare, the floors bare, every sound coming back off the glass. The partition was slid open, so it was all one room. The garden was black behind the glass wall. Mina sat in her father’s place. I sat beside her. She put the cassette into the machine and closed the little door and looked at me, and pressed play.
There was a hiss. A clock ticking, in a room in Santa Monica, forty years ago. A bird.
Then a man’s voice, close to the microphone, saying, I’m warm. Is that — that’s it? That’s all it is?

I have told you what we heard. You have heard it too. You have been hearing it, between the parts of this story, since the night I sat on the kerb at the top of the hill; I have set it down for you in the places where it belongs, the way it came to us that night, in pieces. I did not know, the first time I heard those words, that they were not mine. You did not either. They could have been mine. That was the thing that undid me, sitting at that table. Every word could have been mine.
It went in a week. All of it. I’d been so careful.
So she’ll believe it’s always there. He’ll live inside the wall. In my house. And the other voice, the woman’s, asking him: Will he want to?

Mina sat absolutely still with her hands flat on the table, the way she had put her hand flat on his letter the day the lawyer came, and listened to her father, thirty-five years old, warm and unafraid, telling a stranger the truth.
That I lost it first.
That it was the beginning of me.

Tell her I was never a wall. I was a man standing very still so she wouldn’t see me shaking. And then the thing that had not been in any of the pieces. A long silence on the tape. A breath. And then, very low, a little hoarse, in a voice I had never heard him use, not at the shutter, not at Nowruz, not ever, Mansour Sadri began to sing.
Not the first line. The whole poem.
Ey qowm be hajj rafteh, kojāyid, kojāyid… O you who went away on pilgrimage — where are you, where are you? The one you love is right here. Come back. Come back.
Your beloved is your neighbour, wall to wall with you — why are you wandering, lost, in the desert?
If you could see the face of the one you love, the face that has no face, you would see that you yourselves are the master, and the house, and the holy place.
Ten times you took that road to that house. Once — just once — climb up from this house onto its own roof.

He was crying, on the tape. You could hear it. It did not stop him. It went into the song and the song carried it, the way a river carries a branch. And then he came to the last lines, the ones he had never sung aloud at any shutter, and he sang them very slowly, as if he were reading them for the first time.
For all of that — may your suffering become your treasure. Alas — that you yourselves are the veil over your treasure.
Afsus ke bar ganj-e shomā pardeh shomāyid. [af-SOOS keh bar GANJ-eh sho-MAH par-DEH sho-mah-YEED]
The tape ran on for a few seconds in silence. Then the click.

Mina did not move. The machine hissed. The glass wall held the two of us, sitting at the table in the empty room, the way it had held me alone on the night of the Notice, a man and a woman in the dark looking in.

“He knew,” she said at last. Very quietly. “When he gave me the passwords — no. When he wrote you that letter. Look after it anyway. He knew exactly what you’d do. He knew because he’d done it.” She turned and looked at me, and her face was wrecked and shining. “He wasn’t giving you one more brick, Farzad. He was giving you the hammer.”
I could not answer her. I put my hand over hers on the table.
“You yourselves are the veil over your treasure,” she said. “He sang the beginning of that every morning of my life. He’d sing the first line and stop. And I thought that was all there was.”
The fifteenth of September.

We did not go to Norwalk. There was no reason to. You do not have to watch them sell your house; it happens on the steps of a courthouse twenty miles away, at ten in the morning, in a few minutes, between people you will never meet, and then a man phones a lawyer and the lawyer phones you. We had been told we could stay until the end of the month. We had decided to leave that morning.
So at a quarter to ten we stood in the garden.

The house was empty behind us, swept, the partitions slid open, every room one room, the long glass wall full of sky. The lemon tree stood where Mansour had planted it in 1986, taller than the roof now, heavy with fruit, green and yellow. Mina had cut a branch from it the week before, a short green shoot, and Sunny had shown her how to dip it and pot it, and now it stood in a clay pot of Sunny’s making at Mina’s feet, a stick with four leaves, looking like nothing at all.
“It’ll take,” Sunny said. She had come over barefoot to see us off. “Lemons are stubborn. They don’t know when they’re beaten.”
“Neither did he,” said Mina.

Yasi stood with her bike, her good bike, the one I had bought with a wink, which we had not sold, because she had asked, and because I had said the first true thing to her about it at the market and she had said she wanted to keep it anyway. It’s not the bike’s fault, she had said.

At ten o’clock nobody said anything. We just stood there. A plane went over, low, going down into the airport. Somewhere two gardens away a sprinkler ticked. Somewhere in Norwalk, twenty miles east, on a set of concrete steps, a man was saying a number out loud.
At five past ten, Mina bent down and picked up the pot.
“Let’s go up the hill,” she said.

So we went up Grand View, the four of us, Sunny too, barefoot on the hot pavement, past the shut market street where the canopies would go up again on Sunday, past the houses with their cars nose to tail, up to the crest, where the road tips over. And we turned round.

It was a clear morning. The marine layer had burned off early. The whole west side of the city lay below us, roofs and palms and the long straight cut of Venice Boulevard running down and down, and at the bottom of it all, past the last of the houses, the sea. Not a blade, that morning. Not a hole. Just the sea, enormous and blue and ordinary, with the sun on it, and a few white sails out by the marina, and the long brown line of the beach where, on Sunday, the drums would be.
Mar Vista. Sea view. It was telling the truth.
“He used to bring me up here,” Mina said. “When I was little. On Sundays. He’d stand right here and point at it and say, Look. All the way to the end. And nobody owns it.”
She held the clay pot against her hip with the stick of lemon in it, four leaves turning in the wind off the water.
“I never knew what he meant,” she said. “I thought he was talking about the sea.”
There is a drum circle on the sand at the foot of Horizon Avenue every Sunday, and nobody runs it, and nobody started it, and nobody keeps count.

We went on the first Sunday in October, from the apartment, on our bikes, down the long green path along Ballona Creek where the herons stand on one leg in the concrete as if no one had told them, out between the breakwaters of the marina, up the sand to Venice. Mina had the green scarf on, because a market is a party and so is this. Yasi went straight into the ring and danced at the far side of it, where she could pretend we were not there. She was fifteen. She danced like she was four.
Mina and I sat on the sand at the edge with our shoes off.

We had not taken anything since August. We would not again, we had decided, unless one day we needed to, and then we would drive up the gorge and ask Margaret, if Margaret was still there, and sit in her quiet room in daylight on purpose. It was not a thing for every day. It was a thing for one day. It had turned the lights on in a room we had been walking round in the dark, and we had seen where the furniture was. We were moving it ourselves now. It was heavy. Some days we did it badly. Some nights the old machine in the next room started humming again, don’t, don’t say it, and one of us would hear it, and say, out loud, at the kitchen table in the small apartment over the dry cleaner’s, I can hear it again, and the other would say I know, me too, and that was usually enough.

That is all it does, in the end. I want to be plain about this. It is not magic. It did not save the house. It did not give us back a single dollar. It did one thing, one day, for each of us: it switched off the fear long enough for us to hear what we had been saying underneath it. And then it switched the fear back on, and left us to decide whether to keep talking anyway.
We have kept talking.

The sun went down into the sea, slowly and then all at once, a red coin into a slot. The drums went on in the dark. Somebody lit a fire in a steel bin, which you are not allowed to do, and nobody stopped them.
“Farzad,” Mina said.
“Mm.”
“Sing it.”
I looked at her.

“He sang it when he was nervous,” she said. “Margaret said. Every morning, at the shutter. Because he was frightened. Every single morning of his life, he was frightened, and he sang.” She put her hand on the back of my neck, cold, the way she had in the car on the night I met him. “You’re frightened. I can see it. Sing it.”

So I sang it. Badly, in my bad Persian, with the drums going and the fire crackling and my daughter dancing in the dark on the far side of the ring. Not just the first line. All of it. All the way to the end.
Afsus ke bar ganj-e shomā pardeh shomāyid.

Alas — that you yourselves are the veil over your treasure. Nobody turned to look. That is the thing about the drum circle. Nobody is in charge. Nobody is keeping count. You just come, and you hit something, or you sing something, and it is fine.
That night, in the apartment, after Yasi was asleep, I took Sunny’s old silver tape machine out of the cupboard and put Mansour’s cassette in it, and turned it over.
Side B was blank. Forty years of hiss.

I sat at the small kitchen table in the small kitchen, with the window open on the sound of Venice Boulevard and the smell of the dry cleaner’s steam coming up from below, and I pressed record. And I told it to my daughter, who is asleep, who used to think her father was a wall.

I told her the number. I told her what I did, and why, and the why under the why. I told her about her grandfather, and the silver, and the Thursday, and the shutter, and the song. I told her about her mother, and the window opening a crack, and the word need, said for the first time on a couch in Ojai, clumsily, like a word in a new language.
I told her that I lost it. That I lost it second.
And that it was the beginning of me.

I am telling it to you, too, now. I have been telling it to you all along. I set the pieces of his side down for you where they belong, because I wanted you to hear them the way we did, not knowing whose they were. I wanted you to think they were mine. They were. They are. That is the whole of what I learned, on the hill and in the quiet room and at the table on the last night in his house: the man on the tape and the man at this table are the same man, forty years apart, frightened, standing very still. We are always the same man. We go such a long way to find out.
The one you love is right here.
Come back. Come back. I pressed stop. The little machine clicked. Outside, a bus went down Venice Boulevard toward the sea.
WHAT IT DID
Set down plainly, as a field-worker would: what the substance did in this book.

What it was. MDMA [em-dee-em-AY], first made in a German laboratory in 1912. It was made, not grown, and it is not a vision drug: it shows a person nothing that is not there. It makes the brain release a flood of its own messenger for calm, serotonin [seh-roh-TOH-nin], and turns down the amygdala [uh-MIG-duh-luh], the small almond-shaped knot deep in the brain that listens all day for danger.

Who took it. A man of forty-seven, twice: once by accident at a party, from a stranger’s tin, a dangerous way to do it; once on purpose, in a quiet room in daylight, with an old therapist beside him. His wife, forty-four, once, in the same room. A third, forty years before, heard only on a tape.
The body. Warmth from the hands inward; then heat, its danger. Days later, a flat grey low.

The self. This is the whole of what it did. The fear switched off, the way you notice a machine has been running in the next room only when it stops, and with it went the hand on the throat that puts the safe answer in a person’s mouth. Nothing forced the truth out. Nothing stood in front of it any more.

What it meant. That most of what a person calls himself is the part that is afraid. That honesty is not courage; it is what is left when the fear goes. And that two people can share a house for years, both praying for the same wall to fall.

The cost. Nobody died here. On the record: it can overheat a body, and people at dances have died of the heat, or of drinking too much water trying not to; it strains the heart and clashes with many common medicines; the low days after can be very dark; and what is sold as it is very often something else, now sometimes something that kills. It did one thing, one day, for each of them, and left them to decide whether to keep talking. They did.
THE MAPMAKER

For Leo Zeff and Alexander Shulgin A molecule nobody wanted sat on a shelf in Germany for most of the twentieth century. It had been made at the Merck company in Darmstadt in 1912, as one step on the way to a medicine to stop bleeding, and patented, and forgotten. For years afterwards people said it had been invented as a diet pill. It had not. Even its first story was a mistake.

Alexander Shulgin [SHUL-gin] (1925–2014) was a chemist who left a good job at a large company to work alone, in a small laboratory behind his house in the hills of Lafayette, east of San Francisco. He made new molecules that act on the mind and tried each one on himself, carefully, starting with tiny amounts, and wrote down what happened in plain words, with his wife Ann, who became his partner in the work. He made MDMA again in the mid-1970s and found that it did not show him visions. It did something stranger and quieter: it opened people. He thought it might be useful in therapy, and he gave some to an old friend.

Leo Zeff (1912–1988) was that friend: a psychologist in Oakland, nearly ready to stop working. He tried it, and did not stop. For the next decade he travelled quietly up and down the country teaching other therapists how to sit with a person for a whole day while they took it: in a quiet room, in daylight, on purpose, with someone beside them who would not leave. He is the one usually credited with its old name, Adam, for the way it seemed to return people to the garden before shame. Accounts of how many therapists he taught range from hundreds to thousands; he worked in secret, so nobody kept count. He appears in Myron Stolaroff’s book The Secret Chief (1997) under the name Jacob.

The rest of the story. When the drug got out of therapists’ offices and into nightclubs in Texas, the United States banned it in a hurry, on 1 July 1985. A judge who then heard the doctors’ evidence recommended that it be allowed in medicine anyway; the government overruled him. Decades later, after careful studies with soldiers, firefighters and survivors of violence, Australia let psychiatrists prescribe it in 2023, and in August 2024 the American government looked at the evidence and said not yet.

One of them found the molecule again; the other found out what it was for, and that the room and the people around it mattered as much as the medicine. Between them, without ever quite meaning to, they drew the map of a country most people will never visit: the place a person can stand for one day without being afraid of themselves.
